The Bianchi identity holds for every field, and it is instructive to see it hold for a field with derivatives in all directions. The second exercise checks all components for an explicit potential.

::: {#exr-su2-bianchi}
#### The Bianchi identity on an explicit field

For $A^1_1 = xy$, $A^2_2 = t\sin z$, $A^3_3 = e^x$, compute $F$ and check $D_{[\rho}F_{\mu\nu]} = 0$ for all index
values.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The field strength has derivative terms ($F^1_{01} = -\partial_1 A^1_0 + \dots$) and the commutator term
$F^3_{12} = g\,xy\,t\sin z$; the Bianchi identity holds component by component, as it must for any field. In
Sage (all 192 components):

{{< sage exr-su2-bianchi >}}
:::

The algebraic reason behind the Bianchi identity is the Jacobi identity, and isolating its role is the content of the third exercise. It sorts the terms of the cyclic sum by the number of potentials they contain.

::: {#exr-gth-bianchi-jacobi}
#### The Bianchi identity from the Jacobi identity

Expand $\sum_{\rm cyc}D_\rho F_{\mu\nu} = \sum_{\rm cyc}(\partial_\rho F_{\mu\nu} + [A_\rho, F_{\mu\nu}])$ for $F = dA + [A, A]$
and show that the terms with no potential undifferentiated cancel by symmetry of second derivatives, the terms with
one differentiated and one undifferentiated potential cancel in pairs, and the terms with three potentials cancel by
the Jacobi identity.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Terms in $\partial\partial A$: $\sum_{\rm cyc}\partial_\rho(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu) = 0$ since each $\partial_\rho\partial_\mu A_\nu$
appears once with each sign. Terms in $A\,\partial A$: from $\partial_\rho[A_\mu, A_\nu]$ come $[\partial_\rho A_\mu, A_\nu] +
[A_\mu, \partial_\rho A_\nu]$, and from $[A_\rho, \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu]$ come $[A_\rho, \partial_\mu A_\nu] - [A_\rho,
\partial_\nu A_\mu]$; under the cyclic sum, $[A_\mu, \partial_\rho A_\nu]$ from the first cancels $-[A_\mu, \partial_\rho A_\nu]$
coming from the second with $(\rho, \mu, \nu) \to (\mu, \nu, \rho)$, and similarly for the other pairs. Terms in $AAA$:
$\sum_{\rm cyc}[A_\rho, [A_\mu, A_\nu]] = 0$, the Jacobi identity. For $SU(2)$ the last statement is $\epsilon_{abe}\epsilon_{ecd} +
\epsilon_{bce}\epsilon_{ead} + \epsilon_{cae}\epsilon_{ebd} = 0$, which is the content of @prp-su2-field-strength.
:::
::::

#### Anomaly coefficients

A gauge theory with chiral fermions, left- and right-handed Weyl spinors in different representations, is
consistent as a quantum theory only if a cubic invariant of its fermion representations vanishes. The quantum origin
of the condition, the anomaly, was outlined in quantum field theory (@def-chiral-anomaly); the invariant itself is pure group theory,
and this subsection defines it and computes it for the groups used so far [@nath2017supersymmetry, Secs. 6.1 and
6.9].

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gth-anomaly-coefficient}
#### Anomaly coefficient

Let left-handed Weyl fermions (@def-dq-weyl-equation) transform in a representation $\rho$ of a compact gauge group $G$
(@def-representation), and let $t_a = i\rho(T_a)$ be the Hermitian generators. The **anomaly coefficient** of $\rho$ is the totally
symmetric tensor
$$
d_{abc}(\rho) = \operatorname{Tr}\bigl(t_a\{t_b, t_c\}\bigr) ;
$$ {#eq-gth-anomaly-coefficient}
for $G = U(1)$ and charges $q_k$ it is $2\sum_kq_k^3$. A right-handed fermion in $\rho$ counts as a left-handed fermion in the
**conjugate representation** $\bar\rho(g) = \rho(g)^*$, whose Hermitian generators are $-t_a^T$. A gauge theory is free of gauge
anomalies only if the sum of $d_{abc}$ over all its left-handed fermions vanishes (@def-anomaly).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The abelian case shows the content of the condition most simply. The first example compares a single charged Weyl
fermion with the Dirac fermion of quantum electrodynamics.

::: {#exm-gth-anomaly-u1}
#### Charged Weyl fermions

A single left-handed Weyl fermion of charge $q$ has $d = 2q^3 \neq 0$: a $U(1)$ gauge theory with only this fermion is
inconsistent. A Dirac fermion of charge $q$ is a left-handed Weyl fermion of charge $q$ and a right-handed one of charge $q$,
that is, a left-handed one of charge $-q$, so its total is $2q^3 - 2q^3 = 0$: quantum electrodynamics, in which both
chiralities carry the same charge, is anomaly-free. A cancellation among chiral fermions needs several charges, as in
@exr-gth-anomaly-u1-charges.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $SU(2)$ the Pauli matrices anticommute, and this kills the anomaly coefficient of the doublet outright. The second
example shows it and anticipates the general reason.

::: {#exm-gth-anomaly-su2}
#### $SU(2)$ has no anomaly coefficient

For the doublet $t_a = \tfrac12\sigma_a$ and $\{\sigma_b, \sigma_c\} = 2\delta_{bc}$, so $d_{abc} = \tfrac14\delta_{bc}\operatorname{Tr}\sigma_a = 0$. The same holds for every
representation of $SU(2)$, because each is equivalent to its conjugate (@prp-gth-anomaly-conjugate): the weak
interactions, which act only on left-handed doublets, are free of $SU(2)^3$ anomalies whatever the fermion content.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $SU(3)$ the fundamental representation and its conjugate are inequivalent, and the anomaly coefficient is non-zero.
The third example records it and the way the strong interactions avoid it.

::: {#exm-gth-anomaly-su3}
#### Quarks and $SU(3)$

With the Gell-Mann matrices (@eq-gell-mann), $t_a = \tfrac12\lambda_a$ gives $d_{118}(\mathbf3) = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3} \neq 0$, and $\mathbf{\bar3}$ has the
opposite coefficients (@exr-gth-anomaly-su3). In one generation of the Standard Model the left-handed quark doublet supplies
two triplets and the conjugates $\bar u$, $\bar d$ of the right-handed quarks two antitriplets, so the $SU(3)^3$ coefficients
cancel [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 6.10]: the strong interactions treat both chiralities alike.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The coefficients of $SU(3)$ follow from the Gell-Mann matrices by multiplication and traces. The first exercise
computes them all, for the triplet, the antitriplet and the adjoint.

::: {#exr-gth-anomaly-su3}
#### The anomaly coefficients of $SU(3)$

Compute with Sage all non-zero $d_{abc}(\mathbf3)$, $a \leq b \leq c$, check that $d_{abc}(\mathbf{\bar3}) = -d_{abc}(\mathbf3)$, and that the
adjoint representation $(t_a)_{bc} = -if_{abc}$ has $d_{abc} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The non-zero values are $d_{118} = d_{228} = d_{338} = \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}$, $d_{448} = \dots = d_{778} = -\tfrac{1}{4\sqrt3}$, $d_{888} = -\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3}$
and $\pm\tfrac14$ for $146, 157, 247, 256, 344, 355, 366, 377$, half the usual $d$-symbols because $t_a = \tfrac12\lambda_a$. For $\mathbf{\bar3}$,
$\operatorname{Tr}((-t_a^T)\{-t_b^T, -t_c^T\}) = -\operatorname{Tr}((\{t_b, t_c\}t_a)^T) = -d_{abc}$. The adjoint is real, so its coefficients vanish.

{{< sage exr-gth-anomaly-su3 >}}
:::

For a single $U(1)$ the conditions are two Diophantine equations, the cubic one and the linear one that a coupling to
gravity adds. The second exercise searches for chiral solutions, sets of charges without opposite pairs.

::: {#exr-gth-anomaly-u1-charges}
#### Anomaly-free sets of charges

Left-handed fermions of integer charges $q_1, \dots, q_n$ need $\sum q_k^3 = 0$ and, coupled to gravity, $\sum q_k = 0$. Show that
there is no chiral solution with $n = 3$, and search with Sage for chiral solutions with $|q_k| \leq 9$ and $n \leq 5$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $n = 2$, $q_2 = -q_1$ is vector-like. For $n = 3$ with $q_3 = -q_1 - q_2$, $q_1^3 + q_2^3 + q_3^3 = 3q_1q_2q_3$, which vanishes only if a
charge is zero, and then the other two are opposite. The search finds nothing for $n = 4$ either, and for $n = 5$ the set $(1, 5,
-7, -8, 9)$ and its negative: chiral anomaly-free $U(1)$ theories exist, but they need several fermions with rather special
charges.

{{< sage exr-gth-anomaly-u1-charges >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A product group $G \times U(1)$ has mixed coefficients, with one $U(1)$ generator and two of $G$. The third exercise reduces
them to a sum over representations weighted by their charges.

::: {#exr-gth-anomaly-mixed}
#### Mixed anomalies

Let left-handed fermions transform in representations $\rho_k$ of a simple group $G$ with $U(1)$ charges $q_k$, and let
$\operatorname{Tr}(t_at_b) = T(\rho_k)\delta_{ab}$ in $\rho_k$. Show that the coefficient with one $U(1)$ index and two $G$ indices is $2\sum_kq_kT(\rho_k)\delta_{ab}$,
and that for $SU(2)$ doublets it vanishes exactly when the hypercharges of the doublets add up to zero.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $\rho_k \otimes \mathbb{C}$ the $U(1)$ generator is $q_k\mathbb{1}$, which commutes with the $t_a$, so $\operatorname{Tr}(q_k\{t_a, t_b\}) =
2q_k\operatorname{Tr}(t_at_b) = 2q_kT(\rho_k)\delta_{ab}$, and the total is the sum over $k$. All doublets have the same $T = \tfrac12$, so
the condition is $\sum_{\text{doublets}}q_k = 0$, weighted by the number of colours, the condition of @nath2017supersymmetry
[eq. 6.137] and of @exm-anomaly-standard-model.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

Anomaly coefficients behave simply under the operations that build representations from others, and those rules decide
at once which groups can be anomalous at all. The proposition collects them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-gth-anomaly-conjugate}
#### Anomaly coefficients of conjugates, sums and products

For representations of a compact semisimple group, $d_{abc}(\bar\rho) = -d_{abc}(\rho)$, $d_{abc}(\rho_1 \oplus \rho_2) = d_{abc}(\rho_1) +
d_{abc}(\rho_2)$ and $d_{abc}(\rho_1 \otimes \rho_2) = \dim\rho_2\,d_{abc}(\rho_1) + \dim\rho_1\,d_{abc}(\rho_2)$. In particular a representation
equivalent to its conjugate, a real or pseudo-real one, has $d_{abc} = 0$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 6.9].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Grand unification puts a whole generation into representations of one simple group, and the anomaly must cancel
inside them. The first example shows how it does for $SU(5)$, whose generation is not a single irreducible representation.

::: {#exm-gth-anomaly-su5}
#### One generation of $SU(5)$

In $SU(5)$ grand unification a generation fills $\mathbf{\bar5} \oplus \mathbf{10}$, with $\mathbf{10} = \Lambda^2\mathbf5$ the antisymmetric square. Its
anomaly is that of the $\mathbf5$, $d(\mathbf{10}) = (N - 4)d(\mathbf5) = d(\mathbf5)$ for $N = 5$, while $d(\mathbf{\bar5}) = -d(\mathbf5)$ by the
proposition, so the generation is anomaly-free [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 6.9 and eq. 6.123]; the cancellation among the
quarks and leptons of the Standard Model is this identity restricted to $SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1) \subset SU(5)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For many groups the proposition settles the question once and for all. The second example lists the groups whose gauge
theories cannot have the anomaly of the definition, whatever the fermions.

::: {#exm-gth-anomaly-safe-groups}
#### Groups without anomalies

$SU(2)$, $SO(2N + 1)$, $SO(4N)$, $Sp(N)$, $G_2$, $F_4$, $E_7$ and $E_8$ have only real or pseudo-real representations, so every
$d_{abc}$ vanishes [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 6.125, which lists all $SO(2N)$ here, although the spinors of $SO(4N + 2)$ are complex].
$SO(4N + 2)$ for $N \geq 2$ and $E_6$ have complex representations but no symmetric cubic invariant on their Lie algebras, so
$d_{abc} = 0$ for them too [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 6.126]; the exception $SO(6) \cong SU(4)$ has one and is not safe. This is one reason for the
appeal of $SO(10)$, whose $16$-dimensional spinor representation contains a complete generation with a right-handed
neutrino, and of $E_6$, which appears in heterotic string compactifications.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A vanishing anomaly coefficient does not exhaust the consistency conditions. The third example describes a subtler,
global inconsistency of $SU(2)$, the group that the proposition declares safe.

::: {#exm-gth-witten-anomaly}
#### Witten's $SU(2)$ anomaly

An $SU(2)$ gauge theory with an odd number of left-handed doublets is inconsistent although all $d_{abc} = 0$: the fermion
determinant is defined only up to a sign that flips under a gauge transformation not connected to the identity, which
exists because $\pi_4(SU(2)) = \mathbb{Z}_2$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 6.9.1]. In one generation of the Standard Model there are four
doublets, three of quarks and one of leptons, an even number.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The rule for tensor products follows from the form of the generators on a tensor product. The first exercise proves it and
applies it to the adjoint representation of $SU(N)$.

::: {#exr-gth-anomaly-tensor}
#### Conjugates and tensor products

Prove the three rules of @prp-gth-anomaly-conjugate, using that the generators of a semisimple group are traceless and that
$\rho_1 \otimes \rho_2$ has the generators $t_a \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes t'_a$. Deduce that the adjoint of $SU(N)$, which is $\mathbf N \otimes
\mathbf{\bar N}$ minus a singlet, has $d_{abc} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The conjugate has generators $-t_a^T$, and since the trace of a transpose is the trace,
$d(\bar\rho) = -\operatorname{Tr}(t_a^T\{t_b^T, t_c^T\}) = -\operatorname{Tr}((\{t_b, t_c\}t_a)^T) = -d(\rho)$. Direct sums have block-diagonal generators, so traces add. For the tensor product, $\operatorname{Tr}_{\rho_1 \otimes \rho_2}(X
\otimes Y) = \operatorname{Tr}X\,\operatorname{Tr}Y$; expanding $s_a\{s_b, s_c\}$ with $s_a = t_a \otimes 1 + 1 \otimes t'_a$, the terms with all three factors in
$\rho_1$ give $\dim\rho_2\,d(\rho_1)$, those with all three in $\rho_2$ give $\dim\rho_1\,d(\rho_2)$, and every mixed term contains a single
generator alone in one factor, whose trace vanishes. If $\rho \cong \bar\rho$ then $d(\rho) = d(\bar\rho) = -d(\rho) = 0$, since $d$ is unchanged by a
change of basis. For $SU(N)$, $d(\mathbf N \otimes \mathbf{\bar N}) = N d(\mathbf{\bar N}) + N d(\mathbf N) = 0$, and the singlet contributes nothing.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The antisymmetric representations of $SU(N)$ are the building blocks of most unified models, and their anomaly
coefficients have a closed form. The second exercise checks Nath's formula and finds anomaly-free combinations
[@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 6.123 and Problem 6.7].

::: {#exr-gth-anomaly-antisymmetric}
#### Antisymmetric tensors of $SU(N)$

The representation $[N, k] = \Lambda^k\mathbf N$ has the anomaly $A_N(k)\,d(\mathbf N)$ with $A_N(k) = \frac{(N - 3)!\,(N - 2k)}{(N - k - 1)!\,(k - 1)!}$.
Check the formula with Sage for $N = 4, \dots, 9$ by computing $\operatorname{Tr}(h^3)$ for a traceless diagonal generator $h$, and find
anomaly-free combinations of $[6, 1]$ and $[6, 4]$, and of $[7, 2]$, $[7, 4]$ and $[7, 6]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The weights of $\Lambda^k\mathbf N$ for $h = \operatorname{diag}(a_1, \dots, a_N)$ are the sums of $k$ distinct $a_i$, and since $SU(N)$ has a single
symmetric cubic invariant one generator determines the ratio. The formula holds for all the cases; it gives $A_N(N - k) =
-A_N(k)$, as the proposition requires since $[N, N - k]$ is conjugate to $[N, k]$. For $SU(6)$, $A_6(1) = 1$ and $A_6(4) = -2$, so $2[6, 1]
\oplus [6, 4]$ is anomaly-free; for $SU(7)$, $A_7(2) = 3$, $A_7(4) = -2$ and $A_7(6) = -1$, so $[7, 2] \oplus [7, 4] \oplus [7, 6]$ is. For $SU(5)$
the formula gives $A_5(2) = 1$, the cancellation of @exm-gth-anomaly-su5.

{{< sage exr-gth-anomaly-antisymmetric >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The right-handed quarks of the Standard Model are not optional: without them the strong interactions would be anomalous.
The third exercise makes the count, both with and without them.

::: {#exr-gth-anomaly-colour}
#### Removing a right-handed quark

In one generation the left-handed fermions in coloured representations are the doublet $Q$ (two triplets) and $\bar u$, $\bar d$
(antitriplets). Compute the total $SU(3)^3$ coefficient in units of $d(\mathbf3)$, and the change if the right-handed up quark
were absent. Why does no lepton enter?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The total is $2d(\mathbf3) + 2d(\mathbf{\bar3}) = 2 - 2 = 0$ by @prp-gth-anomaly-conjugate [@nath2017supersymmetry, Sec. 6.10]. Without $\bar u$ it
would be $2 - 1 = 1$ in units of $d(\mathbf3)$, and the theory would be inconsistent: in this sense quantum consistency requires
both chiralities of each quark colour. Leptons are $SU(3)$ singlets, with $d = 0$, and do not contribute.
:::

### Exercises {#sec-gauge-theories-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises that combine the two sections of this part: a charged plane wave in a constant potential, which
uses the covariant derivative and the gauge freedom of the abelian theory; a non-abelian potential along a fixed
generator, where Yang-Mills theory reduces to electromagnetism; and the transport around a small square in a
constant non-abelian potential, which connects the commutator in the field strength to the group commutator.

The first integrative exercise shows that a constant abelian potential is invisible to a single charged field,
because it is pure gauge, although it shifts the momentum. It uses the covariant derivative of the first section
and the gauge transformation of the potential.

::: {#exr-gth-int-plane-wave}
#### A charged plane wave in a constant potential

In scalar electrodynamics with a constant potential $A_\mu = a_\mu$ and $F = 0$, show that $\phi = e^{-ik\cdot x}$ solves
$(D_\mu D^\mu + m^2)\phi = 0$ if and only if $(k - qa)^2 = m^2$. Find the gauge transformation that removes $a_\mu$ and
show that it maps the solution to a free plane wave with momentum $k - qa$. Why can this not be done for a constant
non-abelian potential with $[a_\mu, a_\nu] \neq 0$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$D_\mu e^{-ik\cdot x} = -i(k_\mu - qa_\mu)e^{-ik\cdot x}$, so $D_\mu D^\mu\phi = -(k - qa)^2\phi$ and the equation holds iff $(k -
qa)^2 = m^2$. The potential $a_\mu = \partial_\mu(a\cdot x)$ is pure gauge: with $\alpha = a\cdot x$, $A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha = 0$
and $\phi \mapsto e^{iq\alpha}\phi = e^{-i(k - qa)\cdot x}$, a free plane wave of momentum $p = k - qa$ satisfying $p^2 = m^2$:
the canonical momentum $k$ and the kinetic momentum $p$ differ by $qa$, and only the latter is gauge invariant. A
constant non-abelian potential has $F_{\mu\nu} = [a_\mu, a_\nu] \neq 0$, and @exr-gth-F-not-invariant shows that no gauge
transformation removes it.
:::

The second integrative exercise embeds electromagnetism into $SU(2)$. It uses the non-abelian field strength and
Yang-Mills equations of the second section and the abelian Maxwell equations and charges of the first.

::: {#exr-gth-int-embedded-coulomb}
#### Electromagnetism inside $SU(2)$

Let $A_\mu = a_\mu T_3$ with an abelian potential $a_\mu$. Show that $F_{\mu\nu} = (\partial_\mu a_\nu - \partial_\nu a_\mu)T_3$, that
the Yang-Mills equations reduce to Maxwell's equations for $a_\mu$, and that the components of a doublet couple to
$a_\mu$ with charges $\mp\tfrac12$. Check with Sage that the Coulomb potential $a_0 = Q/r$, $\vec a = 0$, solves the
Yang-Mills equations away from the origin.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[a_\mu T_3, a_\nu T_3] = 0$, so $F = da\,T_3$, and $D_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} + [A_\mu, F^{\mu\nu}] =
(\partial_\mu f^{\mu\nu})T_3$ with $f = da$: Maxwell's equations. On a doublet, $a_\mu T_3 = -\tfrac{i}{2}a_\mu\sigma_3 =
\operatorname{diag}(-\tfrac i2, \tfrac i2)a_\mu$, which is $iqa_\mu$ with $q = -\tfrac12$ for the upper and $q = +\tfrac12$ for the
lower component. The Coulomb potential gives the radial field $\vec E = Q\vec x/r^3$ along $T_3$, and $\nabla^2(1/r) = 0$
away from the origin.

{{< sage exr-gth-int-embedded-coulomb >}}
:::

The third integrative exercise interprets the commutator term of the field strength as the failure of transports
along two directions to commute. It uses the gauge group elements of the second section, the constant
configuration of @exm-su2-constant and the abelian holonomy of @exr-gth-pure-gauge-abelian.

::: {#exr-gth-int-group-commutator}
#### Transport around a small square

For the constant potential $A_1 = c_1T_1$, $A_2 = c_2T_2$, the transport along a side of length $\epsilon$ in the
direction $i$ is $g_i = e^{\epsilon A_i}$. Show with Sage that $g_1g_2g_1^{-1}g_2^{-1} = 1 + \epsilon^2F_{12} +
O(\epsilon^3)$ with $F_{12} = [A_1, A_2] = c_1c_2T_3$, and that for two potentials along $T_3$ the product is exactly $1$.
Interpret the result.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $X = \epsilon A_1$, $Y = \epsilon A_2$, $e^Xe^Ye^{-X}e^{-Y} = 1 + [X, Y] + O(\epsilon^3)$, so the product is $1 +
\epsilon^2c_1c_2T_3 + O(\epsilon^3)$. When both potentials lie along $T_3$ the exponentials commute and the product is
$1$. The product of transports around the boundary of a small square is $1$ plus the field strength times the area:
the field strength is the holonomy per unit area, and for a constant non-abelian potential it is non-zero because
transports in different directions do not commute, while for a constant abelian potential it vanishes, as in
@exr-gth-pure-gauge-abelian where only a non-contractible loop sees a flat potential.

{{< sage exr-gth-int-group-commutator >}}
:::
::::

## Gauge fields as connections {#sec-gauge-connections}

The first part built gauge fields from a requirement: a derivative that transforms like the field. The mathematics part has already met the same objects from the other side, as connections on principal bundles, with their curvature, their gauge transformations and their holonomy (@sec-connections). This part puts the two descriptions side by side. It says which physical object is which geometric one, and it then uses the geometric notion that the first part did not need, transport along a finite path. Transport around a closed loop gives the holonomy, and its trace gives the Wilson loop, the gauge-invariant quantity that the lattice formulation later in the chapter takes as its basic observable and that the Aharonov-Bohm effect of the next part measures.

For more on this topic, see @hamilton2017mathematical [Ch. 4-5] and @guidry2022symmetry [Ch. 26].

The conventions are those of the chapter. Generators are anti-Hermitian, a field in a representation $\rho$ transforms as $\phi \mapsto \rho(g)^{-1}\phi$, and $D_\mu\phi = \partial_\mu\phi + \rho(A_\mu)\phi$; for $U(1)$ and charge $q$, $\rho(A_\mu) = iqA_\mu$ with real $A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$, and $\hbar = c = 1$ in Heaviside-Lorentz units. The transporter of a field along a path is written as a path-ordered exponential of $-\int A$, the sign of @def-gauge-potential and of @hamilton2017mathematical [Sec. 5.10].

### Connections and associated bundles {#sec-gcn-connections}

![The holonomy of a square of side $L$ in the constant $SU(2)$ potential $A_x = T_1$, $A_y = T_2$, for which $F_{xy} = [A_x, A_y] = T_3$. Left: the Wilson loop $\frac12 W(C) = \frac14 + \cos L - \frac14\cos 2L$ of the doublet, against the value $\cos(L^2/2)$ that a naive abelian Stokes theorem $\operatorname{Hol} = e^{-L^2F_{xy}}$ would give; the two agree to order $L^4$ and then separate. Right: the deviation of the holonomy from $1 - L^2F_{xy}$ falls like $L^3$, so the field strength is the holonomy per unit area. Generated by `figures/gcn_wilson_square.sage`.](figures/gcn_wilson_square.svg){#fig-gcn-wilson-square width=95%}

In the first part the gauge potential was a field on spacetime with a transformation law, and the field strength was read off a commutator of covariant derivatives (@exr-commutator-covariant, @exm-covariant-commutator). Both were already identified, one block at a time, with the gauge potential and the curvature of a connection (@def-gauge-field-u1, @def-nonabelian-field-strength). This section states the identification once and in full, and then shows what it buys: global questions, such as whether a potential exists on all of spacetime or whether two potentials describe the same field, become questions about bundles.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gcn-gauge-field}
#### Gauge field as a connection

Let $P \to M$ be a principal $G$-bundle over spacetime (@def-principal-bundle) with a connection $\omega$ (@def-bundle-connection). In a gauge theory with gauge group $G$, the **gauge field** is the connection $\omega$, and the gauge potential $A_\mu$ of @def-nonabelian-gauge-field is its pullback $A = s^*\omega = A_\mu dx^\mu$ by a local section $s$ (@def-gauge-potential). The other objects of the theory are identified as follows:

- the field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$ of @def-nonabelian-field-strength is the curvature of $\omega$ (@def-curvature-connection), pulled back by $s$;
- a gauge transformation $g(x)$ is a change of local section $s \mapsto s\,g$, under which $A$ changes by @eq-gauge-transformation;
- a matter field in a representation $\rho$ of $G$ on $V$ is a section $[s, \phi]$ of the associated vector bundle $P \times_\rho V$ (@exm-vector-bundle-associated), written in the section $s$ as a function $\phi\colon U \to V$; since $[s, \phi] = [s\,g, \rho(g)^{-1}\phi]$, it changes as $\phi \mapsto \rho(g)^{-1}\phi$, and $D_\mu\phi = \partial_\mu\phi + \rho(A_\mu)\phi$ is the covariant derivative that the connection induces on the associated bundle.

For $G = U(1)$ and a field of charge $q$, $\rho(e^{i\theta}) = e^{iq\theta}$, the connection pulls back to $iqA_\mu dx^\mu$ in the representation of charge $q$, and the gauge parameter $\alpha$ of @def-gauge-field-u1 is the change of section by $g = e^{-i\alpha}$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Defs. 5.4.1 and 5.6.1, Thms. 5.4.2 and 5.6.3, Remark 5.4.3; @guidry2022symmetry, Sec. 26.3].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The simplest gauge theory is electromagnetism on Minkowski space, where the bundle is a product and a single section covers everything. The first example translates its potential and its fields into the language of the definition.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-electromagnetism}
#### Electromagnetism

Minkowski space is contractible, so every $U(1)$-bundle over it is trivial, $P = \mathbb{R}^4 \times U(1)$, and $s(x) = (x, 1)$ is a global section. The connection pulls back to $iA_\mu dx^\mu$ with $A_\mu = (\Phi, -\vec A)$ the potentials of @def-emm-potentials, and its curvature is $iF_{\mu\nu}$, whose components are $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ (@exr-gth-maxwell-from-fields). Because $U(1)$ is abelian, $F$ does not depend on the section, so $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ are gauge invariant, while the potentials change by @def-emm-gauge-transformation [@hamilton2017mathematical, Def. 5.7.1 and the remark after it].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The product bundle carries a connection of its own, the one whose horizontal directions are those of the base. In the section that defines the product it has vanishing potential, and in every other section it has a pure gauge potential.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-trivial}
#### The product connection

On $P = M \times G$ declare the tangent spaces of the slices $M \times \{h\}$ horizontal. In the section $s(x) = (x, 1)$ the potential is $A = 0$; in the section $s\,g$ it is $g^{-1}dg$ by @eq-gauge-transformation, the pure gauge potential of @exm-pure-gauge, and the curvature vanishes in every section. A potential is pure gauge exactly when it describes this connection in some section.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Fields of different charge couple to the same electromagnetic field. In the language of bundles they are sections of different associated bundles of one principal bundle, as the next example explains.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-charges}
#### Charges as representations

The irreducible representations of $U(1)$ are $\rho_q(e^{i\theta}) = e^{iq\theta}$, and $\rho_q$ is well defined on $U(1)$ only for $q \in \mathbb{Z}$, in units of a smallest charge. Fields of charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ are sections of the line bundles $P \times_{\rho_{q_1}}\mathbb{C}$ and $P \times_{\rho_{q_2}}\mathbb{C}$, and their product has charge $q_1 + q_2$ because $\rho_{q_1}\rho_{q_2} = \rho_{q_1 + q_2}$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Example 4.7.16]. Taking the gauge group to be $U(1)$ rather than the real line is thus already a statement that charges are commensurate; the monopole of the next part forces the same conclusion dynamically.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a non-abelian group the representation matters even more, because the potential acts on the field by matrices. The doublet and the triplet of $SU(2)$ are the two cases used throughout the chapter.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-su2}
#### Doublets and triplets of $SU(2)$

For $G = SU(2)$ a doublet is a section of $P \times_\rho \mathbb{C}^2$ with the defining representation, and $\rho(A_\mu) = A^a_\mu T_a$ acts by $2 \times 2$ matrices, as in @exm-covariant-doublet. A triplet is a section of the adjoint bundle $P \times_{\mathrm{Ad}}\mathfrak{su}(2)$, written as $\Phi = \Phi^aT_a$ with $\mathrm{Ad}(A_\mu)\Phi = [A_\mu, \Phi]$ (@exm-covariant-adjoint-scalar). The same connection defines both covariant derivatives.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The field strength transforms by conjugation, unlike the potential, and this has a global meaning. The next example states it and draws the consequence for the colour-electric and colour-magnetic fields.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-adjoint-valued}
#### The field strength lives in the adjoint bundle

Under $s \mapsto s\,g$ the pulled-back curvature changes as $F \mapsto g^{-1}Fg$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Thm. 5.6.3], so the local field strengths glue to a two-form with values in the adjoint bundle, not in a fixed vector space. For $U(1)$ the conjugation is trivial and $F$ is an ordinary closed two-form on $M$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Cor. 5.6.4]. For $SU(3)$ the chromo-electric and chromo-magnetic fields $F_{0i}$ and $F_{ij}$ are not gauge invariant; only quantities such as $\operatorname{tr}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ are.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

When no global section exists, the potential is given chart by chart. The next example says how the potentials on two overlapping charts are related, which is the situation of the magnetic monopole.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-transition}
#### Potentials on two charts

If $s_i$ and $s_j$ are local sections on overlapping open sets, $s_i = s_j\,g_{ji}$ on the overlap with the transition function $g_{ji}$ (@def-transition-function), and the potentials are related by $A_i = g_{ji}^{-1}A_jg_{ji} + g_{ji}^{-1}dg_{ji}$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Thm. 5.4.2]. The gauge transformation between two charts is the transition function: the bundle is encoded in how the potentials are glued, and a non-trivial bundle needs at least two potentials.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Flatness is a local property and triviality a global one. The next example records when the first implies the second, which is the hypothesis that the Aharonov-Bohm effect violates.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-flat}
#### Flat connections on simply connected spaces

If $F = 0$ on a connected and simply connected region $U$, horizontal lifts of loops in $U$ close, so transporting a point of the fibre from a base point along any path gives a well-defined section with $A = 0$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Exercise 5.15.4]. Every flat potential on such a region is pure gauge. Outside a solenoid the region is not simply connected and the conclusion fails (@exr-gth-pure-gauge-abelian).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

There are two ways of describing a gauge transformation, by changing the section or by moving the points of the bundle. The next example compares them.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-active-passive}
#### Passive and active gauge transformations

A change of section $s \mapsto s\,g$ leaves the connection alone and changes its description, the passive view. A bundle automorphism $f\colon P \to P$ commuting with the group action changes the connection to $f^*\omega$ and leaves the sections alone, the active view; in a section the two give the same formula @eq-gauge-transformation [@hamilton2017mathematical, Thm. 5.4.4 and the remark after it]. Physical statements are invariant under both.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Standard Model at the end of the chapter has a product gauge group and many matter fields. In the language of the definition it is one principal bundle with many associated bundles.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-standard-model}
#### One bundle, many matter fields

The Standard Model has one principal bundle with group $SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$ and one connection, whose components are the gluons, the $W$ bosons and the hypercharge boson. Each quark and lepton field is a section of the bundle associated with its own representation, listed in the Standard Model section below. The covariant derivatives of all of them come from the one connection, which is why a single coupling constant per factor governs every matter field.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In Kaluza-Klein theory the bundle is not added to spacetime but is spacetime. The last example points ahead to Part III, where this is the starting point.

::: {#exm-gcn-gf-kk}
#### The bundle as spacetime

A five-dimensional spacetime $M \times S^1$ is a principal $U(1)$-bundle over $M$, with the circle acting by translation of the fifth coordinate. A metric with off-diagonal components $g_{\mu 5}$ defines a connection on it, whose horizontal directions are those orthogonal to the circle, and its potential is $A_\mu$ (@exm-potential-kk, @exm-gauge-field-kk). Part III starts from this observation: the gauge field is part of the geometry of a higher-dimensional spacetime.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises start with the transformation law in the simplest case and end with the invariance of the Yang-Mills Lagrangian. The first translates the change of section into the gauge transformation of @def-gauge-field-u1.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-section-change}
#### The abelian transformation from a change of section

For $G = U(1)$ and a field of charge $q$, apply @eq-gauge-transformation with $g = e^{-i\alpha(x)}$ to the potential $iqA_\mu dx^\mu$ in the representation of charge $q$, and show that $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$ and $\phi \mapsto e^{iq\alpha}\phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For an abelian group $g^{-1}Ag = A$, and $\rho(g)^{-1}d\rho(g) = e^{iq\alpha}d(e^{-iq\alpha}) = -iq\,d\alpha$. So $iqA_\mu \mapsto iqA_\mu - iq\partial_\mu\alpha$, which is $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$, and $\phi \mapsto \rho(g)^{-1}\phi = e^{iq\alpha}\phi$: the transformation of @def-gauge-field-u1 and @def-covariant-derivative-u1.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A pure gauge potential can look complicated while carrying no field. The second exercise computes one for $SU(2)$ and checks that its curvature vanishes.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-pure-gauge}
#### A pure gauge $SU(2)$ potential

For $g(x, y) = e^{xT_1}e^{yT_2}$, compute $A = g^{-1}dg$ and show with Sage that $A_y = T_2$, $A_x = \cos y\,T_1 + \sin y\,T_3$, and $F_{xy} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_yg = gT_2$, so $A_y = T_2$. $\partial_xg = T_1g$, so $A_x = g^{-1}T_1g = e^{-yT_2}T_1e^{yT_2}$, the rotation of $T_1$ about the $2$-axis, which is $\cos y\,T_1 + \sin y\,T_3$ by @eq-su2-brackets. Then $\partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x + [A_x, A_y] = -(-\sin y\,T_1 + \cos y\,T_3) + \cos y\,[T_1, T_2] + \sin y\,[T_3, T_2] = \sin y\,T_1 - \cos y\,T_3 + \cos y\,T_3 - \sin y\,T_1 = 0$. The potential is the product connection of @exm-gcn-gf-trivial in the section $s\,g$.

{{< sage exr-gcn-gf-pure-gauge >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The transformation of matter fields follows from the definition of the associated bundle rather than being postulated. The third exercise derives it and the covariance of the covariant derivative.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-associated}
#### Matter fields from the associated bundle

The associated bundle identifies $(p, v)$ with $(p\,h, \rho(h)^{-1}v)$ for $h \in G$. Show that a section written as $[s, \phi]$ is written as $[s\,g, \rho(g)^{-1}\phi]$ in the section $s\,g$, and that $D_\mu\phi$ transforms as $\phi$ does when $A$ changes by @eq-gauge-transformation.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$[s, \phi] = [s\,g\,g^{-1}, \phi] = [s\,g, \rho(g)^{-1}\phi]$, using the identification with $h = g$. With $\phi' = \rho(g)^{-1}\phi$ and $\rho(A'_\mu) = \rho(g)^{-1}\rho(A_\mu)\rho(g) + \rho(g)^{-1}\partial_\mu\rho(g)$, and $\partial_\mu\rho(g)^{-1} = -\rho(g)^{-1}\partial_\mu\rho(g)\rho(g)^{-1}$,
$$
\partial_\mu\phi' + \rho(A'_\mu)\phi' = \rho(g)^{-1}\partial_\mu\phi - \rho(g)^{-1}\partial_\mu\rho(g)\rho(g)^{-1}\phi + \rho(g)^{-1}\rho(A_\mu)\phi + \rho(g)^{-1}\partial_\mu\rho(g)\rho(g)^{-1}\phi = \rho(g)^{-1}D_\mu\phi .
$$
The derivative terms of $g$ cancel, as in @def-covariant-derivative-nonabelian.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The field strength is covariant but not invariant. The fourth exercise checks both statements on an explicit potential and gauge transformation.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-curvature-covariance}
#### The field strength under a change of section

For the $SU(2)$ potential $A_x = y\,T_3$, $A_y = x\,T_1$ compute $F_{xy}$. For $g = e^{xT_2}e^{xyT_3}$ compute $A' = g^{-1}Ag + g^{-1}dg$ and its field strength, and show with Sage that $F'_{xy} = g^{-1}F_{xy}g \neq F_{xy}$ while $\operatorname{tr}F'^2_{xy} = \operatorname{tr}F^2_{xy}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{xy} = \partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x + [A_x, A_y] = T_1 - T_3 + xy[T_3, T_1] = T_1 + xy\,T_2 - T_3$. The transformed field strength is the conjugate, as @hamilton2017mathematical [Thm. 5.6.3] states; its components differ from those of $F$, since conjugation rotates them in the adjoint representation, but the trace of the square, $-\frac12(2 + x^2y^2)$, is unchanged.

{{< sage exr-gcn-gf-curvature-covariance >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The abelian case is special because the field strength is a global object even when the potential is not. The fifth exercise proves this and identifies what remains local.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-abelian-global}
#### The abelian field strength is global

For $G = U(1)$, show that the local field strengths $F_i = dA_i$ agree on overlaps and define a closed two-form on $M$. Show by an example on $S^2$ that this two-form need not be $dA$ for a global one-form $A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On an overlap $A_i = A_j + g_{ji}^{-1}dg_{ji}$ (@exm-gcn-gf-transition), and for $g_{ji} = e^{i\lambda}$ the extra term is $i\,d\lambda$, whose exterior derivative vanishes; so $dA_i = dA_j$ and the local forms glue to a global $F$, closed because $dF = ddA_i = 0$ locally. On $S^2$ the Hopf curvature $F = -\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$ has $\int_{S^2}F = -4\pi \neq 0$, so by Stokes it is not $dA$ for a global $A$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Cor. 5.6.4 and Remark 5.6.5; @exr-emm-pot-no-global].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A bundle over a single point has only one connection. The sixth exercise identifies it and reads its flatness as a familiar equation.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-point}
#### The bundle over a point

Consider $G$ as a principal $G$-bundle over a point, with $G$ acting by right multiplication. Show that the Maurer-Cartan form $g^{-1}dg$ is a connection and the only one, and that its curvature vanishes by the Maurer-Cartan equation @eq-maurer-cartan.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every tangent vector is vertical, so the horizontal subspaces are zero and the connection form must restrict to the Maurer-Cartan form on the fibre, which is all of $G$: there is no choice. Its curvature is $d(g^{-1}dg) + g^{-1}dg \wedge g^{-1}dg = -g^{-1}dg \wedge g^{-1}dg + g^{-1}dg \wedge g^{-1}dg = 0$, the Maurer-Cartan equation [@hamilton2017mathematical, Exercise 5.15.5]. The pure gauge potentials of @exm-gcn-gf-trivial are pullbacks of this form by $g\colon M \to G$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Charges must be integers in units of a smallest charge once the gauge group is $U(1)$. The seventh exercise makes the argument precise.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-integer-charges}
#### Why charges are integers

Show that $\rho_q(e^{i\theta}) = e^{iq\theta}$ is a well-defined representation of $U(1)$ if and only if $q \in \mathbb{Z}$, but a representation of the real line for every real $q$. If a theory contains charges $\frac23$ and $-\frac13$ in units of $e$, what is the smallest unit in which $U(1)$ can be the gauge group?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$e^{i\theta}$ and $e^{i(\theta + 2\pi)}$ are the same element of $U(1)$, so $e^{iq\theta} = e^{iq(\theta + 2\pi)}$ is required, that is $e^{2\pi iq} = 1$ and $q \in \mathbb{Z}$; on the real line there is no identification and every $q$ gives a representation. With charges $\frac23$ and $-\frac13$ the unit must divide both, so it is at most $\frac13$: in units of $e/3$ the charges are $2$ and $-1$, integers, and $U(1)$ with the generator normalised to $e/3$ is the gauge group. Charges in an irrational ratio would force the real line instead.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The adjoint representation acts on the Lie algebra by conjugation, and its derivative is the commutator. The eighth exercise checks this and the covariance of the adjoint covariant derivative.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-adjoint}
#### The adjoint covariant derivative

For $SU(2)$ show that $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tX}\Phi e^{-tX}\big|_{t = 0} = [X, \Phi]$, so the adjoint representation of the algebra is $\mathrm{ad}(X)\Phi = [X, \Phi]$. For $A = x\,T_3 + T_1$ along one coordinate $x$, $\Phi = x^2T_1 + \sin x\,T_2$ and $g = e^{x^2T_2}e^{xT_3}$, check with Sage that $D\Phi = \partial_x\Phi + [A, \Phi]$ transforms as $\Phi' = g^{-1}\Phi g$ does, while $\partial_x\Phi$ does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Differentiating $e^{tX}\Phi e^{-tX}$ at $t = 0$ gives $X\Phi - \Phi X$. In the adjoint representation $\rho(g)^{-1}\Phi = g^{-1}\Phi g$, and @exr-gcn-gf-associated with $\rho = \mathrm{Ad}$ gives $D'\Phi' = g^{-1}(D\Phi)g$; the plain derivative picks up $[g^{-1}\partial_xg, \Phi']$, which the commutator with the transformed potential cancels.

{{< sage exr-gcn-gf-adjoint >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The proof that flat connections on simply connected regions are trivial uses transport along paths. The ninth exercise carries it out for $U(1)$, where it reduces to the Poincaré lemma.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-flat-trivial}
#### Flat and simply connected means pure gauge

Let $U$ be connected and simply connected, and $A = A_idx^i$ a real one-form on $U$ with $dA = 0$. Fix $x_0 \in U$ and define $\lambda(x) = \int_\gamma A$ for a path $\gamma$ from $x_0$ to $x$. Show that $\lambda$ does not depend on $\gamma$ and that $A = d\lambda$. Conclude that the $U(1)$ potential $A$ is the gauge transform of $0$ by $\alpha = -\lambda$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Two paths $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$ form a loop $\gamma_1\gamma_2^{-1}$, which bounds a surface $S$ in $U$ because $U$ is simply connected; by Stokes (@thm-stokes) $\int_{\gamma_1}A - \int_{\gamma_2}A = \int_S dA = 0$. Differentiating $\lambda$ along a short straight segment at $x$ gives $\partial_i\lambda = A_i$. With @def-gauge-field-u1, $0 \mapsto 0 - \partial_i(-\lambda) = A_i$. The non-abelian version replaces the integral by the transporter along $\gamma$, which is path independent by the same argument [@hamilton2017mathematical, Exercise 5.15.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Yang-Mills Lagrangian is built from a field strength that changes under gauge transformations. The last exercise shows that the Lagrangian itself is a function on spacetime.

::: {#exr-gcn-gf-yang-mills-density}
#### The Yang-Mills density is gauge invariant

Show that $\operatorname{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$ is unchanged by $F \mapsto g^{-1}Fg$, so that the Yang-Mills action of @def-yang-mills-action is defined independently of the section. With $\operatorname{tr}(T_aT_b) = -\frac12\delta_{ab}$, express it through the components $F^a_{\mu\nu}$, and check with Sage for $SU(2)$ that $\operatorname{tr}$ of products of components is invariant while the component $F^3$ is not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\operatorname{tr}(g^{-1}F_{\mu\nu}g\,g^{-1}F^{\mu\nu}g) = \operatorname{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$ by cyclicity of the trace, at each point; so the local Lagrangians agree on overlaps and define a function on $M$, which is the global content of @exm-gcn-gf-adjoint-valued. With $F = F^aT_a$, $\operatorname{tr}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = -\frac12F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\,\mu\nu}$. A rotation mixes the components, so $F^3$ alone changes.

{{< sage exr-gcn-gf-yang-mills-density >}}
:::

### Holonomy and Wilson loops {#sec-gcn-holonomy}

A connection compares fibres at neighbouring points, and integrating the comparison along a path compares fibres at distant points. The first part used only the infinitesimal version, the covariant derivative; @exm-gth-parallel-transport derived it from transport over a distance $dx$. This section integrates. Transport along a path is a group element that depends on the path, transport around a loop is the holonomy, and the trace of the holonomy is a gauge-invariant number, the Wilson loop. The abelian holonomy around a loop is the Aharonov-Bohm phase of @prp-qcp-aharonov-bohm, and the definition makes this precise.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gcn-holonomy}
#### Holonomy of a gauge field

Let $A$ be a gauge field with a potential defined along a curve $\gamma\colon[0, 1] \to M$, and $\rho$ a representation. The **parallel transporter** along $\gamma$ is
$$
U_\gamma = \mathcal P\exp\Big(-\int_\gamma\rho(A)\Big) ,
$$ {#eq-gcn-transporter}
the value at $t = 1$ of the solution of $\frac{d}{dt}U(t) = -\rho\bigl(A_\mu(\gamma(t))\bigr)\dot\gamma^\mu(t)\,U(t)$ with $U(0) = 1$; the **path ordering** $\mathcal P$ puts the potential at later points of the path to the left. A field carried along $\gamma$ by $\phi(t) = U(t)\phi(\gamma(0))$ is covariantly constant, $\dot\gamma^\mu D_\mu\phi = 0$. The transporter does not depend on the parametrisation, satisfies $U_{\gamma_2\gamma_1} = U_{\gamma_2}U_{\gamma_1}$ for $\gamma_1$ followed by $\gamma_2$ and $U_{\gamma^{-1}} = U_\gamma^{-1}$, and transforms as
$$
U_\gamma \mapsto \rho\bigl(g(\gamma(1))\bigr)^{-1}\,U_\gamma\,\rho\bigl(g(\gamma(0))\bigr) .
$$ {#eq-gcn-transporter-gauge}
For a loop $C$ based at $x_0$, $U_C = \operatorname{Hol}_{x_0}(C)$ is the **holonomy** of $C$, and it changes by conjugation. For $U(1)$ and charge $q$, $\operatorname{Hol}(C) = e^{-iq\oint_CA_\mu dx^\mu}$, which for a spatial loop in a static field is $e^{iq\oint_C\vec A\cdot d\vec l}$, the phase @eq-qcp-ab-phase with $\hbar = 1$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Secs. 5.8 and 5.10, Thm. 5.10.5, Def. 5.11.1 and Prop. 5.11.2; @guidry2022symmetry, eqs. (26.6)-(26.10), with Hermitian generators and the opposite orientation].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For an abelian group the matrices of the potential commute, and the path ordering does nothing. The first example writes the abelian transporter and recognises it in quantum mechanics.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-u1}
#### The abelian transporter is a phase

For $U(1)$ and charge $q$, the equation $\dot U = -iqA_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu U$ has the solution $U_\gamma = e^{-iq\int_\gamma A_\mu dx^\mu}$, with no ordering needed. Along a spatial path in a static field, $-A_idx^i = \vec A\cdot d\vec x$ and $U_\gamma = e^{iq\int_\gamma\vec A\cdot d\vec l}$: the factor by which @eq-qcp-ab-solution multiplies the free wave function [@guidry2022symmetry, Example 26.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

When the potential is constant along a straight segment, the ordering is harmless even for a non-abelian group, because the potential commutes with itself. This is the case that the lattice uses on every link.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-constant}
#### A straight segment in a constant potential

If $A_\mu$ is constant and $\gamma(t) = x_0 + tLn$ with a unit vector $n$, then $\rho(A_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu = L\rho(A_\mu)n^\mu$ is a constant matrix and $U_\gamma = e^{-L\rho(A_\mu)n^\mu}$. The link variable $e^{aA_\mu}$ of the lattice section below is the transporter along the same link traversed backwards, from $x + a\hat\mu$ to $x$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A pure gauge potential transports by the gauge function itself. The third example computes the transporter and concludes that every loop has trivial holonomy.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-pure-gauge}
#### Transport in a pure gauge potential

For $A = g^{-1}dg$ in a representation $\rho$, $U(t) = \rho(g(\gamma(t)))^{-1}\rho(g(\gamma(0)))$ solves the transport equation, since $\dot U = -\rho(g)^{-1}\tfrac{d}{dt}\rho(g)\,U = -\rho(A_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu U$. So $U_\gamma = \rho(g(\gamma(1)))^{-1}\rho(g(\gamma(0)))$ depends only on the endpoints, and $\operatorname{Hol}(C) = 1$ for every loop: the trivial potential transformed by @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The transporter along a time-like path at a fixed point of space is not a geometric curiosity: it is the time evolution of a static charge. The fourth example computes it in an electrostatic potential.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-time}
#### Transport in time is the energy

For the path $t \mapsto (t, \vec x)$ with $t \in [0, T]$, a charge $q$ in a static potential $\Phi$ has $U = e^{-iq\int_0^TA_0\,dt} = e^{-iq\Phi(\vec x)T}$, the phase $e^{-iET}$ of a state of energy $E = q\Phi(\vec x)$. The time component of the transporter records the potential energy of a static charge, which is how the Wilson loop measures the potential between two charges (@exm-gcn-wl-static).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Paths can be joined and reversed, and the transporter respects both operations. The fifth example uses this to compare holonomies based at different points of the same loop.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-base-point}
#### Changing the base point

Let $C$ be a loop through $x$ and $y$, with $\gamma$ the part from $x$ to $y$ and $\gamma'$ the part from $y$ back to $x$. Then $\operatorname{Hol}_x(C) = U_{\gamma'}U_\gamma$ and $\operatorname{Hol}_y(C) = U_\gamma U_{\gamma'} = U_\gamma\operatorname{Hol}_x(C)U_\gamma^{-1}$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Lemma 5.11.3]. Holonomies at different base points are conjugate, so their eigenvalues and traces agree.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The holonomy of a small loop is close to the identity, and the deviation is the field strength times the area. The sixth example states this, which is the precise sense in which the field strength is a curvature.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-small-loop}
#### Small loops measure the field strength

For the square $C$ of side $\epsilon$ in the $(\mu, \nu)$ plane, traversed first along $\mu$, $\operatorname{Hol}(C) = 1 - \epsilon^2\rho(F_{\mu\nu}) + O(\epsilon^3)$ (@exr-gcn-hol-small-square, @fig-gcn-wilson-square). For $U(1)$ in the $xy$ plane, $-iqF_{xy} = -iq(\partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x) = iqB_z$, and the holonomy is $1 + iq\epsilon^2B_z$, as in @exr-qcp-ab-small-loop; for constant non-abelian potentials it is the group commutator of @exr-gth-int-group-commutator.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In a uniform magnetic field the holonomy of a planar loop depends only on its area. The seventh example states the result, which is behind the degeneracy of Landau levels.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-uniform-B}
#### A uniform magnetic field

For $\vec B = B\hat z$, every counterclockwise loop in a plane of constant $z$ enclosing the area $\mathcal A$ has $\operatorname{Hol} = e^{iqB\mathcal A}$ in every gauge (@exr-gcn-hol-uniform-field). The holonomy is $1$ exactly for areas that are multiples of $2\pi/qB$, the area per state of a Landau level in @prp-qcp-landau-levels.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Levi-Civita connection of a surface is a connection on its frame bundle, with structure group $SO(2)$. Its holonomy is the rotation of a vector carried around a loop, and the eighth example recalls it on the sphere.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-sphere}
#### Holonomy on the sphere

Parallel transport of a tangent vector around the parallel $\theta = \theta_0$ of the unit sphere (@def-parallel-transport, @exr-parallel-transport) returns it rotated by the angle $2\pi\cos\theta_0$, or equivalently by $-2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$, minus the area of the enclosed cap. This is the holonomy of the $SO(2) \cong U(1)$ connection of the frame bundle of the sphere, the gravitational counterpart of the Aharonov-Bohm phase [@guidry2022symmetry, Sec. 26.1.3].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A non-abelian potential along a single generator behaves like an abelian one. The ninth example computes its transporter on a doublet and identifies the charges of the two components.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-embedded}
#### A potential along one generator

If $A_\mu = a_\mu(x)T_3$ for $SU(2)$, the matrices at different points commute and $U_\gamma = e^{-T_3\int_\gamma a}$. On a doublet $T_3 = \operatorname{diag}(-\frac i2, \frac i2)$, so $U_\gamma = \operatorname{diag}\bigl(e^{\frac i2\int_\gamma a}, e^{-\frac i2\int_\gamma a}\bigr)$: the two components are transported as charges $-\frac12$ and $+\frac12$ of the abelian potential $a_\mu$, as in @exr-gth-int-embedded-coulomb.
:::

The transporter depends on the path, and the dependence is measured by a holonomy. The last example makes the relation explicit.

::: {#exm-gcn-hol-path-dependence}
#### Path dependence is holonomy

For two paths $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$ from $x$ to $y$, $U_{\gamma_2}^{-1}U_{\gamma_1} = U_{\gamma_2^{-1}\gamma_1}$ is the holonomy at $x$ of the loop out along $\gamma_1$ and back along $\gamma_2$. Transport is path independent in a region exactly when all holonomies there are trivial; by @exm-gcn-gf-flat this holds for a flat connection on a simply connected region, and it fails outside a solenoid.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The exercises begin with the abelian transporter and its gauge transformation and end with the covariant derivative recovered from transport. The first checks the transport equation for $U(1)$.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-ode}
#### The abelian transport equation

Show that $U(t) = e^{-iq\int_0^tA_\mu(\gamma(s))\dot\gamma^\mu(s)\,ds}$ solves $\dot U = -iqA_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu U$ with $U(0) = 1$, and that $\phi(t) = U(t)\phi_0$ satisfies $\dot\gamma^\mu D_\mu\phi = 0$ in the sense $\dot\phi + iqA_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu\phi = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By the chain rule $\dot U = -iqA_\mu(\gamma(t))\dot\gamma^\mu(t)\,U$, and $U(0) = e^0 = 1$. Then $\dot\phi = \dot U\phi_0 = -iqA_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu\phi$, which is $\dot\phi + iqA_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu\phi = 0$, the component of @eq-covariant-derivative-u1 along the curve.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A gauge transformation acts on the transporter only at the endpoints. The second exercise proves this for $U(1)$ by integrating.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-gauge-u1}
#### The abelian transporter under gauge transformations

Under $A_\mu \mapsto A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha$, show that $U_\gamma \mapsto e^{iq\alpha(\gamma(1))}U_\gamma e^{-iq\alpha(\gamma(0))}$, and check that this is @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge with $g = e^{-i\alpha}$. Why is the holonomy of a loop gauge invariant even when $\alpha$ is only defined up to $2\pi/q$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$-iq\int_\gamma(A_\mu - \partial_\mu\alpha)dx^\mu = -iq\int_\gamma A_\mu dx^\mu + iq\bigl(\alpha(\gamma(1)) - \alpha(\gamma(0))\bigr)$, which gives the stated law [@guidry2022symmetry, Example 26.2, with the opposite sign of the gauge function]. With $\rho(g) = e^{-iq\alpha}$, $\rho(g)^{-1} = e^{iq\alpha}$, as in @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge. For a loop the two factors are $e^{iq\alpha(x_0)}$ and $e^{-iq\alpha(x_0)}$ after going around, which cancel as long as $e^{iq\alpha}$ is single valued, even if $\alpha$ itself changes by a multiple of $2\pi/q$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For a non-abelian potential the transporter has to be computed numerically in general. The third exercise does so in two ways and compares them.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-numerical}
#### Computing a transporter

For the $SU(2)$ potential $A_x = \cos y\,T_1$, $A_y = x\,T_3$ and the straight path from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$, compute $U_\gamma$ with Sage by solving the transport equation and as an ordered product of many short exponentials. Check that the two agree, that $U_\gamma \in SU(2)$, and that the unordered $e^{-\int_\gamma A}$ is different.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along $x = y = t$, $A_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu = \cos t\,T_1 + t\,T_3$, whose values at different $t$ do not commute. The ordered product $\prod_k e^{-hA_\mu\dot\gamma^\mu(t_k)}$, with later factors to the left, converges to the solution of the equation, and both are unitary with determinant $1$ because each factor is. The unordered exponential differs at the level of a few per cent, the size of the commutator terms.

{{< sage exr-gcn-hol-numerical >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The transformation law @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge is the defining property of a transporter. The fourth exercise proves it in general by uniqueness of solutions of differential equations.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-endpoints}
#### Only the endpoints feel the transformation

Let $U(t)$ solve the transport equation for $A$, and let $A' = g^{-1}Ag + g^{-1}dg$. Show that $U'(t) = \rho(g(\gamma(t)))^{-1}U(t)\rho(g(\gamma(0)))$ solves the equation for $A'$ with $U'(0) = 1$, and conclude @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Write $G(t) = \rho(g(\gamma(t)))$. Then $\dot U' = -G^{-1}\dot GG^{-1}UG(0) + G^{-1}\dot UG(0) = -G^{-1}\dot G\,U' - G^{-1}\rho(A_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu G\,U' = -\rho(A'_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu U'$, using $\rho(A'_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu = G^{-1}\rho(A_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu G + G^{-1}\dot G$. Also $U'(0) = G(0)^{-1}G(0) = 1$. By uniqueness $U'$ is the transporter of $A'$, and at $t = 1$ this is @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge [@guidry2022symmetry, Problem 26.4; @hamilton2017mathematical, Exercise 5.15.9].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Transport along a reversed path undoes transport along the path. The fifth exercise proves this and the independence of the parametrisation.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-reverse}
#### Reversal and reparametrisation

Show that reparametrising $\gamma$ by an increasing function $t = f(s)$ does not change $U_\gamma$, and that $U_{\gamma^{-1}} = U_\gamma^{-1}$ for the reversed path $\gamma^{-1}(t) = \gamma(1 - t)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $V(s) = U(f(s))$, $V' = f'\dot U = -\rho(A_\mu)\frac{d\gamma^\mu}{ds}V$, the same equation in the new parameter, with the same initial value; so the final values agree. For the reversed path, $W(t) = U(1 - t)U(1)^{-1}$ has $W(0) = 1$ and $\dot W = -\dot U(1 - t)U(1)^{-1} = \rho(A_\mu)\dot\gamma^\mu(1 - t)W = -\rho(A_\mu)\frac{d}{dt}\gamma^\mu(1 - t)\,W$, the transport equation along $\gamma^{-1}$; so $U_{\gamma^{-1}} = W(1) = U(1)^{-1}$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Thm. 5.8.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A statement about small loops is easiest to believe after watching the limit happen numerically. The sixth exercise tests the statement of @exm-gcn-hol-small-loop on a potential that is neither constant nor abelian.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-small-square}
#### The holonomy of a small square

For the $SU(2)$ potential $A_x = xy\,T_1$, $A_y = x\,T_2 + T_3$, compute $F_{xy}$ at the origin. Compute the holonomy of the square $[0, \epsilon]^2$, traversed counterclockwise from the origin, with Sage for $\epsilon = 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025$, and show that $(\operatorname{Hol} - 1)/\epsilon^2 \to -F_{xy}(0)$ with an error of order $\epsilon$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{xy} = \partial_xA_y - \partial_yA_x + [A_x, A_y] = T_2 - x\,T_1 + xy[T_1, xT_2 + T_3]$, which is $T_2$ at the origin. Expanding the four transporters to second order, the first-order terms cancel around the loop, and the second-order terms combine into $-\epsilon^2F_{xy}$ at a point of the square; the error of order $\epsilon$ comes from the variation of $F$ across the square. The computed deviation halves with $\epsilon$.

{{< sage exr-gcn-hol-small-square >}}
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The holonomy is gauge invariant, so it must not depend on the choice of potential for a given field. The seventh exercise checks this for a uniform field in two gauges.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-uniform-field}
#### A uniform field in two gauges

For $\vec B = B\hat z$, compute with Sage the circulation of the symmetric potential $\vec A = \frac B2(-y, x, 0)$ and of the Landau potential $\vec A = (0, Bx, 0)$ around the triangle with vertices $(0, 0)$, $(2, 0)$, $(0, 1)$ and around the ellipse $(a\cos t, b\sin t)$. Show that both give $B$ times the area, and hence the holonomy $e^{iqB\mathcal A}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The two potentials differ by $\nabla(Bxy/2)$, a single-valued gauge function, so their circulations around any loop agree. By Stokes the circulation is the flux $B\mathcal A$, which is $B$ for the triangle of area $1$ and $\pi abB$ for the ellipse. The computation confirms it in both gauges.

{{< sage exr-gcn-hol-uniform-field >}}
:::

**Sage.** Pending.

The path ordering is the difference between a gauge field and a collection of commuting phases. The eighth exercise shows how much it matters for a constant $SU(2)$ potential.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-ordering}
#### Three paths to the same point

For $A_x = c\,T_1$, $A_y = c\,T_2$, write the transporters from $(0, 0)$ to $(L, L)$ along $x$ then $y$, along $y$ then $x$, and along the diagonal. Show that they differ, and with Sage that the holonomy of the triangle out along $x$ then $y$ and back along the diagonal is $1 - \frac{L^2}{2}F_{xy} + O(L^3)$ with $F_{xy} = c^2T_3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exm-gcn-hol-constant and composition, the transporters are $e^{-LA_y}e^{-LA_x}$, $e^{-LA_x}e^{-LA_y}$ and $e^{-L(A_x + A_y)}$. They differ because $[A_x, A_y] = c^2T_3 \neq 0$, and the holonomy of the triangle, $e^{L(A_x + A_y)}e^{-LA_y}e^{-LA_x}$, is $1 - \frac{L^2}{2}[A_x, A_y]$ to second order by the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula: the field strength times the area $L^2/2$, as @exm-gcn-hol-small-loop says.

{{< sage exr-gcn-hol-ordering >}}
:::

The temporal gauge $A_0 = 0$ is used in the canonical quantisation of gauge fields. The ninth exercise reaches it with a transporter.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-temporal}
#### Reaching the temporal gauge

On $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^3$, let $g(t, \vec x) = U_{\gamma_{t,\vec x}}$ with $\gamma_{t, \vec x}$ the time-like path from $(0, \vec x)$ to $(t, \vec x)$, in the defining representation. Show that the transformed potential has $A'_0 = 0$. On a spacetime with periodic Euclidean time of length $\beta$, what obstructs this, and what survives?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along the time line $U(t)$ solves $\partial_tU = -A_0U$ with $U = 1$ at $t = 0$. With $g = U$, $g^{-1}A_0g = U^{-1}A_0U$ and $g^{-1}\partial_tg = U^{-1}\partial_tU = -U^{-1}A_0U$, so $A'_0 = g^{-1}A_0g + g^{-1}\partial_tg = 0$. With periodic time, $g$ must also be periodic, which requires the holonomy around the time circle to be $1$; in general $A_0$ can only be made constant in time, and the holonomy around the time circle, the Polyakov loop of the lattice section below, survives as a gauge-covariant variable.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The covariant derivative was the starting point of the first part. The last exercise recovers it from transport, as @exm-gth-parallel-transport did infinitesimally.

::: {#exr-gcn-hol-derivative}
#### The covariant derivative from the transporter

Let $\gamma_\epsilon$ be the straight path from $x + \epsilon\hat\mu$ to $x$. Show that $U_{\gamma_\epsilon} = 1 + \epsilon\rho(A_\mu(x)) + O(\epsilon^2)$ and that
$$
\lim_{\epsilon \to 0}\frac{U_{\gamma_\epsilon}\phi(x + \epsilon\hat\mu) - \phi(x)}{\epsilon} = D_\mu\phi(x) .
$$
Why does the numerator transform like $\phi(x)$ for every $\epsilon$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Along $\gamma_\epsilon$, $\dot\gamma = -\epsilon\hat\mu$, so to first order $U = 1 - \rho(A_\mu)(-\epsilon) = 1 + \epsilon\rho(A_\mu)$. Then $U\phi(x + \epsilon\hat\mu) - \phi(x) = \epsilon(\partial_\mu\phi + \rho(A_\mu)\phi) + O(\epsilon^2)$. By @eq-gcn-transporter-gauge, $U_{\gamma_\epsilon}\phi(x + \epsilon\hat\mu) \mapsto \rho(g(x))^{-1}U_{\gamma_\epsilon}\rho(g(x + \epsilon\hat\mu))\rho(g(x + \epsilon\hat\mu))^{-1}\phi(x + \epsilon\hat\mu)$, so both terms of the numerator transform with $\rho(g(x))^{-1}$: this is the covariant difference that the lattice section takes as its derivative.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Holonomies change by conjugation and are therefore not gauge invariant for a non-abelian group. Their traces are, and they are the observables that survive when everything gauge dependent is discarded. The definition names them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-gcn-wilson-loop}
#### Wilson loop

For a loop $C$ and a representation $\rho$ of the gauge group, the **Wilson loop** is
$$
W_\rho(C) = \operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hol}(C) = \operatorname{tr}\mathcal P\exp\Big(-\oint_C\rho(A)\Big) .
$$ {#eq-gcn-wilson-loop}
It does not depend on the base point on $C$, and it is gauge invariant. For $U(1)$ and charge $q$, $W_q(C) = e^{-iq\oint_CA_\mu dx^\mu}$, and for a spatial loop in a static field $W_q(C) = e^{iq\Phi_B(C)}$, with $\Phi_B(C)$ the magnetic flux through a surface bounded by $C$. For an open path $\gamma$ the transporter $U_\gamma$ is the **Wilson line**. The lattice Wilson loop of @sec-lgt-confinement is the expectation value of $\frac1N\operatorname{Re}W_\rho(C)$ for the defining representation of dimension $N$ [@hamilton2017mathematical, Def. 5.11.4 and Prop. 5.11.5; @guidry2022symmetry, Problem 26.5].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $U(1)$ there is no trace to take and no ordering to worry about, so the Wilson loop is the holonomy itself. The abelian Wilson loop is the exponential of a flux. The first example uses Stokes' theorem to see it.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-flux}
#### The abelian Wilson loop is a flux

For a spatial loop $C = \partial S$ in a static field, $W_q(C) = e^{iq\oint_C\vec A\cdot d\vec l} = e^{iq\int_S\vec B\cdot d\vec S}$ by Stokes (@thm-stokes). It depends on the flux only modulo $2\pi/q$, and it sees the flux through $S$ even when $\vec B = 0$ on $C$ itself.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The trace depends on the representation, and different representations see different parts of the holonomy. The second example compares the trivial, the defining and the adjoint representations of $SU(2)$.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-representations}
#### Wilson loops of $SU(2)$

Every element of $SU(2)$ is conjugate to $e^{\theta T_3}$, $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$, and the Wilson loop depends only on $\theta$: $W_1 = 1$ for the trivial representation, $W_{\mathbf 2} = 2\cos\frac\theta2$ for the doublet and $W_{\mathbf 3} = 1 + 2\cos\theta = W_{\mathbf 2}^2 - 1$ for the adjoint (@exr-gcn-wl-su2-classes). $W_{\mathbf 2}$ is real because $U$ and $U^{-1}$ are conjugate in $SU(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Traversing a loop backwards inverts the holonomy, and for unitary representations the trace of the inverse is the complex conjugate. The third example interprets this.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-orientation}
#### Reversing the loop

$W_\rho(C^{-1}) = \operatorname{tr}\operatorname{Hol}(C)^{-1} = \overline{W_\rho(C)}$ for a unitary representation, which is $W_{\bar\rho}(C)$ for the conjugate representation. For $SU(3)$ the loop traversed by a quark one way equals the loop traversed by an antiquark the other way, and the two differ by complex conjugation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The holonomy of a constant non-abelian potential around a square is not the exponential of the flux. The fourth example compares the two in the configuration of @fig-gcn-wilson-square.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-square}
#### No naive Stokes theorem

For $A_x = T_1$, $A_y = T_2$ the square of side $L$ has $\operatorname{Hol} = e^{LA_y}e^{LA_x}e^{-LA_y}e^{-LA_x}$ and $\frac12W_{\mathbf 2} = \frac14 + \cos L - \frac14\cos 2L$, while $\frac12\operatorname{tr}e^{-L^2F_{xy}} = \cos\frac{L^2}2$. They agree to order $L^4$ and separate at order $L^6$ (@fig-gcn-wilson-square): the non-abelian Stokes theorem needs an ordering of the field strength over the surface, which the abelian flux does not.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Wilson loop that lies in a time-space plane measures the energy of static charges. The fifth example computes it in a static external potential.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-static}
#### A rectangle in time and space

Take the rectangle $C$ in the $(x, t)$ plane through $(0, 0)$, $(R, 0)$, $(R, T)$, $(0, T)$, in a static potential $\Phi(x)$ with $A_x = 0$. The spatial sides contribute nothing and the time sides give $W_q(C) = e^{-iqT(\Phi(R) - \Phi(0))}$: the phase $e^{-iT\Delta E}$ of the energy difference of a charge at $R$ and one at $0$ (@exr-gcn-wl-electric-rectangle). In the quantum theory and in Euclidean time the same rectangle gives $e^{-TV(R)}$, the definition of the static potential in @sec-lgt-confinement.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On a compact direction the Wilson loop is a gauge-invariant field of the lower-dimensional theory. The sixth example computes the abelian case, where the potential itself is periodic.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-circle}
#### Around a compact dimension

On $M \times S^1$ with circle coordinate $y \in [0, 2\pi R)$ and a constant $U(1)$ potential $A_y = a$, the loop around the circle has $W_q = e^{-2\pi iqRa}$. The gauge function $\alpha = ny/(qR)$ has single-valued $e^{iq\alpha} = e^{iny/R}$ and shifts $a$ by $-n/(qR)$ (@exr-gcn-wl-large-gauge): $a$ is defined only modulo $1/(qR)$, and $W_q$ is the gauge-invariant variable. Part III meets this as the Wilson line of the Kaluza-Klein circle.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

In an abelian theory the Wilson loops determine the field strength and the topological data. The seventh example says how.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-determine}
#### Wilson loops determine an abelian field

For $U(1)$ the Wilson loops of small loops give $F_{\mu\nu}$ at every point (@exm-gcn-hol-small-loop), and in a simply connected region the field strength gives every Wilson loop by Stokes. In a region that is not simply connected the loops around the holes add the information that $F$ misses, the Aharonov-Bohm phases; together they fix the potential up to gauge transformations (@exr-gcn-wl-abelian-determines).
:::

**Sage.** Pending.

A potential along one generator gives a Wilson loop that is the trace of a diagonal matrix. The eighth example computes it for the doublet.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-embedded}
#### A Wilson loop along $T_3$

For $A_\mu = a_\mu T_3$, @exm-gcn-hol-embedded gives $\operatorname{Hol}(C) = \operatorname{diag}(e^{\frac i2\Phi_a}, e^{-\frac i2\Phi_a})$ with $\Phi_a = \oint_Ca$, so $W_{\mathbf 2}(C) = 2\cos\frac{\Phi_a}2$. A flux $\Phi_a = 2\pi$ gives $W_{\mathbf 2} = -2$: the holonomy is $-1$, the non-trivial element of the centre of $SU(2)$, which the doublet sees and the adjoint does not (@exr-abm-ab-nonabelian-flux).
:::

A Wilson line between two charged fields makes a gauge-invariant composite. The ninth example builds it, the continuum form of a meson.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-meson}
#### A charge and an anticharge joined by a line

For a field $\phi$ in a unitary representation and a path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$, $\phi(y)^\dagger U_\gamma\phi(x)$ is gauge invariant (@exr-gcn-wl-open-line): the transporter carries the charge at $x$ to $y$, where it meets the conjugate charge [@guidry2022symmetry, Example 26.2]. For quarks this is a quark and an antiquark joined by a string of gauge field, the static meson of the lattice section.
:::

The expectation value of a Wilson loop is the quantity that distinguishes confining from non-confining phases. The last example points to where the chapter computes it.

::: {#exm-gcn-wl-quantum}
#### Wilson loops in the quantum theory

In the quantum theory the gauge field fluctuates and $W_\rho(C)$ becomes a gauge-invariant operator [@hamilton2017mathematical, Sec. 5.11]. In Euclidean space its expectation value decays with the area enclosed by $C$ in a confining theory and with its perimeter otherwise; the lattice section below computes $\langle W\rangle$ for $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $U(1)$ and $SU(2)$ and finds the area law at strong coupling.
:::
