:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The finite-volume statement follows from the invariance of the Haar measure. The first exercise proves it for a single link in detail.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-haar}
#### The link on a finite lattice

On a finite lattice, change variables by the gauge transformation with $g(x) = h$ at one endpoint $x$ of the link and $g = 1$ elsewhere, and show that $\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle = h^{-1}\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle$ for all $h \in G$. Conclude $\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Wilson action and the Haar measure are invariant, so $\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle = \langle g(x)^{-1}U_\mu(x)g(x + a\hat\mu)\rangle = h^{-1}\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle$. Integrating over $h$, $\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle = \bigl(\int dh\,h^{-1}\bigr)\langle U_\mu(x)\rangle = 0$, since $\int dh\,h = 0$ for the matrices of a non-trivial irreducible representation (@exr-lgt-sc-integrals).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In finite volume every expectation value is that of the gauge average of the observable. The second exercise proves this projection property.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-projection}
#### Only the invariant part counts

For any bounded function $O$ of the links on a finite lattice, let $\bar O = \int\prod_xdg(x)\,O[U^g]$ be its average over all gauge transformations. Show that $\langle O\rangle = \langle\bar O\rangle$, and that $\bar O$ is gauge invariant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For each fixed $g$, $\langle O[U^g]\rangle = \langle O\rangle$ by the invariance of the action and the measure; averaging over $g$ gives $\langle\bar O\rangle = \langle O\rangle$ (exchanging the integrals). For a gauge transformation $k$, $\bar O[U^k] = \int dg\,O[U^{kg}] = \bar O[U]$ by the invariance of the Haar measure on the product group.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The bound of the theorem is the heart of the infinite-volume statement. The third exercise derives it in the form @eq-lgt-elitzur-bound.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-bound}
#### The Elitzur bound

Carry out the proof of @thm-lgt-elitzur: show that $\langle O\rangle_J = \bigl\langle\int dg\,O[U^g]e^{-\Delta_g(U)}\bigr\rangle_J$, with $\Delta_g(U) = J\sum_{\ell \ni K}\frac1N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(U_\ell - U^g_\ell)$, and deduce @eq-lgt-elitzur-bound.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Substituting $U \to U^g$ in the integrals for $Z_J\langle O\rangle_J$, with $g$ supported on $K$, leaves the measure and $S_W$ unchanged and changes the source term by $\Delta_g$, so $\langle O\rangle_J = \langle O[U^g]e^{-\Delta_g}\rangle_J$; averaging over $g$ gives the stated form. Subtracting $\langle\int dg\,O[U^g]\rangle_J = 0$, $|\langle O\rangle_J| \leq \sup|O|\sup_{g, U}|e^{-\Delta_g} - 1| \leq \sup|O|(e^{2n_KJ} - 1)$, since each of the $n_K$ terms of $\Delta_g$ lies in $[-2J, 2J]$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $\mathbb{Z}_2$ the averaging over the gauge transformation at one site can be done exactly, and it gives a sharper bound. The fourth exercise derives it and checks it with Sage by enumeration.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-z2-bound}
#### An exact identity for $\mathbb{Z}_2$

In the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory with the source $J\sum_\ell\sigma_\ell$, pair each configuration with the one reversed at the site $x$ (an endpoint of $\ell$), and show $\langle\sigma_\ell\rangle_J = \langle\sigma_\ell\tanh(Js_x)\rangle_J$, where $s_x$ is the sum of the $2d$ links at $x$, so that $|\langle\sigma_\ell\rangle_J| \leq \tanh(2dJ)$. Check both with Sage on the $3 \times 3$ torus at $\beta = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The reversal at $x$ preserves the plaquette term and changes the source by $-2Js_x$; averaging $\sigma_\ell e^{Js_x}$ over the pair $(+, -)$ of each orbit gives $\sigma_\ell\frac{e^{Js_x} - e^{-Js_x}}{e^{Js_x} + e^{-Js_x}}$ with the weight $e^{Js_x} + e^{-Js_x}$, which is the identity, and $|\tanh(Js_x)| \leq \tanh(2dJ)$. The enumeration confirms the identity exactly and the bound:

{{< sage exr-lgt-el-z2-bound >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The Higgs field of a lattice Higgs model is the matter analogue of the link. The fifth exercise shows that its expectation value vanishes, while a gauge-invariant composite does not.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-higgs-zero}
#### The lattice abelian Higgs model

For a $U(1)$ lattice Higgs model with a field $\phi(x)$ of charge one and the action $-\kappa\sum_{x, \mu}H_\mu(x) + \sum_xV(|\phi(x)|^2)$ plus the Wilson action, where $H_\mu(x) = \operatorname{Re}\phi(x)^*e^{i\theta_\mu(x)}\phi(x + a\hat\mu)$, show that $\langle\phi(x)\rangle = 0$, and that $\langle H_\mu(x)\rangle > 0$ for small $\kappa > 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The gauge transformation $e^{-i\alpha}$ at $x$ alone multiplies $\phi(x)$ by $e^{i\alpha}$ and preserves the action and the measure, so $\langle\phi(x)\rangle = e^{i\alpha}\langle\phi(x)\rangle$ for all $\alpha$, hence $0$. The hopping term $H_\mu(x)$ is gauge invariant, and to first order in $\kappa$, $\langle H_\mu(x)\rangle = \kappa\langle H_\mu(x)^2\rangle_0 + O(\kappa^2) > 0$, since at $\kappa = 0$ the phases of the fields and the link are independent and uniform, so that $\langle H_\mu(x)\rangle_0 = 0$ and $\langle H_\mu(x)H_\nu(y)\rangle_0 = 0$ unless the two terms coincide.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The theorem rests on a counting of the terms that a transformation changes. The sixth exercise compares the counts for a global and a local transformation.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-global-vs-local}
#### Counting changed terms

On an $L^d$ lattice with a link source, how many source terms does a gauge transformation at one site change? How many does a global transformation $g(x) = h$ for all $x$ change in a lattice Higgs model with a site source $h\sum_x\operatorname{Re}\phi(x)$? Explain why the bound @eq-lgt-elitzur-bound has no analogue for the global case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A gauge transformation at one site changes the $2d$ link terms at that site, a number independent of $L$. A global transformation changes all $L^d$ site source terms, and the corresponding bound would be $e^{2L^dh} - 1$, useless in infinite volume: the weights of a configuration and its global transform can differ by a factor that grows exponentially with the volume, which is what pins the system in one ordered state.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Averaging a gauge-variant quantity over random gauge transformations makes it vanish, while invariant quantities are untouched. The seventh exercise illustrates this with Sage for $SU(2)$.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-gauge-average}
#### Averaging over random gauge transformations

With Sage, take a fixed $U \in SU(2)$, average $g(x)^{-1}Ug(y)$ over $n = 10^2, 10^4, 10^6$ pairs of Haar-random $g(x), g(y)$, and compare the norm of the average with $1/\sqrt n$. Do the same for $\frac12\operatorname{Tr}g^{-1}U_Pg$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The averaged link decreases like $1/\sqrt n$, the behaviour of a mean of random vectors with zero expectation, while the trace of the conjugated plaquette does not change at all:

{{< sage exr-lgt-el-gauge-average >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For an adjoint Higgs field the gauge-invariant order parameters are the traces of its powers. The eighth exercise computes the cubic one for two vacua of $SU(3)$.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-adjoint-invariants}
#### The cubic invariant

With $T_a = -\frac i2\lambda_a$, compute $\operatorname{Tr}T_8^3$ and $\operatorname{Tr}T_3^3$, and explain why $\operatorname{Tr}\Phi^3$ distinguishes the vacua $vT_8$ and $vT_3$ while $\operatorname{Tr}\Phi^2$ does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\lambda_8 = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\operatorname{diag}(1, 1, -2)$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}\lambda_8^3 = \frac{1 + 1 - 8}{3\sqrt3} = -\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$ and $\operatorname{Tr}T_8^3 = \frac{i}{8}\operatorname{Tr}\lambda_8^3 = -\frac{i}{4\sqrt3}$, while $\lambda_3 = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, 0)$ gives $\operatorname{Tr}T_3^3 = 0$. Both have $\operatorname{Tr}T_a^2 = -\frac12$, so $\operatorname{Tr}\Phi_0^2 = -\frac{v^2}{2}$ in both cases. The eigenvalues of $vT_8$ have a repeated pair, with stabiliser $SU(2) \times U(1)$, those of $vT_3$ are distinct, with stabiliser $U(1) \times U(1)$, and the cubic invariant tells them apart.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The order of the limits decides whether a symmetry breaks. The ninth exercise compares the three cases, the Ising chain, the two-dimensional Ising model and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory, with Sage.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-ising-limits}
#### The order of limits

With Sage, evaluate at $K = 0.5$ and $h = 0.1, 0.01, 0.001$ the magnetisation $m(h) = \frac{\sinh h}{\sqrt{\sinh^2h + e^{-4K}}}$ of the infinite Ising chain, the spontaneous magnetisation $(1 - \sinh^{-4}2K)^{1/8}$ of the two-dimensional Ising model, and the bound $\tanh(4h)$ on a link of the two-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory with source $h$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The chain's magnetisation vanishes linearly in $h$ (no breaking in one dimension), the two-dimensional Ising model keeps $m = 0.911$ (breaking of a global symmetry), and the gauge link is bounded by $\tanh4h \to 0$ (no breaking of a local symmetry, in any dimension):

{{< sage exr-lgt-el-ising-limits >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On a finite periodic lattice even the global centre symmetry is unbroken, and the Polyakov loop averages to zero. The tenth exercise checks this by enumeration with Sage, together with the correlator of two loops.

::: {#exr-lgt-el-polyakov-torus}
#### Polyakov loops on a small torus

For the two-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory on a torus of $4$ sites in space and $2$ in time, enumerate the $2^{16}$ configurations with Sage, compute $\langle P(0)\rangle$ and $\langle P(0)P(R)\rangle$ for $R = 1, 2$ at $\beta = 0.5$ and $1.5$, and compare the correlator with $\frac{s^mc^{n - m} + c^ms^{n - m}}{c^n + s^n}$, $c = \cosh\beta$, $s = \sinh\beta$, $n = 8$, $m = 2R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\langle P\rangle = 0$ exactly, by the centre symmetry of @exr-lgt-z2-polyakov, while the correlator is the product of the plaquettes in the strip between the loops, or in its complement, and matches the formula; at $\beta = 1.5$ it stays close to $1$ on this small torus because $\tanh^{m}\beta$ is not small:

{{< sage exr-lgt-el-polyakov-torus >}}

### Monte Carlo updates of link variables {#sec-lgt-monte-carlo}

![Heat-bath Monte Carlo of the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ gauge theory on a periodic $6^3$ lattice. Left: the average plaquette from cold starts (all links $+1$, circles) and hot starts (random links, crosses), with the strong-coupling series $t + 2t^5$, $t = \tanh\beta$ (dashed), the weak-coupling series $1 - 8e^{-8\beta} - 88e^{-12\beta}$ (dotted) and the critical coupling $\beta_c = 0.761$ given by duality with the Ising model. Right: the plaquette of successive configurations at $\beta = 0.76$; the cold start is close to equilibrium at once, the hot start needs some $50$ sweeps, and near $\beta_c$ the fluctuations are slow. Generated by `figures/lgt_z2_monte_carlo.sage`.](figures/lgt_z2_monte_carlo.svg){#fig-lgt-z2-monte-carlo width=95%}

Outside two dimensions and the strong- and weak-coupling limits, lattice gauge theories are computed by Monte Carlo, as the scalar theory of @def-fpi-metropolis was: configurations are generated by a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is $e^{-S_W}\prod dU/Z$, and expectation values are averages over the chain. The chain changes one link at a time, and the change of the action involves only the plaquettes through that link. The definition isolates the part of the action that a single link sees.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lgt-staple}
#### Staple

For the link $(x, \mu)$, the **staple sum** is
$$
\Sigma_\mu(x) = \sum_{\nu \neq \mu}\Bigl(U_\nu(x + a\hat\mu)U_\mu(x + a\hat\nu)^{-1}U_\nu(x)^{-1} + U_\nu(x + a\hat\mu - a\hat\nu)^{-1}U_\mu(x - a\hat\nu)^{-1}U_\nu(x - a\hat\nu)\Bigr),
$$ {#eq-lgt-staple}
the sum of the $2(d - 1)$ products of three links, the **staples**, that close $U_\mu(x)$ into the plaquettes containing it (@fig-lgt-lattice). The Wilson action depends on $U_\mu(x)$ only through
$$
S_W = -\frac\beta N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(U_\mu(x)\Sigma_\mu(x)\bigr) + (\text{terms independent of } U_\mu(x))
$$ {#eq-lgt-staple-action}
[@boudreau2018applied, eq. 24.43 and Fig. 24.6].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $\mathbb{Z}_2$ each staple is a sign, and their sum is an integer. The first example lists its values, which a program can tabulate in advance.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-z2}
#### The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ staple

For $\mathbb{Z}_2$ in three dimensions there are four staples, each $\pm1$, so $s = \Sigma_\mu(x) \in \{-4, -2, 0, 2, 4\}$ and the local action is $-\beta\sigma_\mu(x)s$. The weights $e^{\pm\beta s}$ take only five values, which @boudreau2018applied [Sec. 24.3.1] store in a table before the simulation.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $U(1)$ the staple sum is a complex number. Its modulus and phase are all that the conditional distribution of the link depends on.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-u1}
#### The $U(1)$ staple

For $U(1)$, $\Sigma_\mu(x) = ke^{i\varphi}$ with $k \geq 0$, and the local action is $-\beta k\cos(\theta_\mu(x) + \varphi)$: the link angle sees a cosine potential centred at $-\varphi$, of strength $\beta k$ [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 24.4.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $SU(2)$ the staple sum is a real combination of $SU(2)$ matrices, which by @exm-lgt-su2-sum is a multiple of one. The third example writes the local action in this form.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-su2}
#### The $SU(2)$ staple

For $SU(2)$, $\Sigma_\mu(x) = kV$ with $k = \sqrt{\det\Sigma_\mu(x)}$ and $V \in SU(2)$, and the local action is $-\beta k\,a_0(U_\mu(x)V)$, with $a_0 = \frac12\operatorname{Tr}$: the link is pulled towards $V^{-1}$, with strength $\beta k$ [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 24.5.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The number of staples grows with the dimension. The fourth example counts them, and with them the cost of computing the staple sum.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-count}
#### How many staples

Each link lies in $2(d - 1)$ plaquettes (@exm-lgt-plaq-count), so there are $2$, $4$ and $6$ staples in two, three and four dimensions, each a product of three links. For $SU(3)$ in four dimensions a staple sum costs $12$ products of $3 \times 3$ complex matrices, each of $27$ complex or $108$ real multiplications, about $1300$ real multiplications per link, the dominant cost of an update.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The simplest update is a Metropolis step, as for the scalar field. The staple makes the change of the action cheap to compute.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-metropolis}
#### A Metropolis update of a link

Propose $U' = XU_\mu(x)$ with $X$ drawn from a distribution on $G$ concentrated near $1$ and symmetric under $X \mapsto X^{-1}$, and accept with probability $\min(1, e^{-\Delta S})$, where $\Delta S = -\frac\beta N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((U' - U_\mu(x))\Sigma_\mu(x)\bigr)$ by @eq-lgt-staple-action. This is @def-fpi-metropolis with the uniform proposal on an interval replaced by a symmetric proposal on the group, which preserves detailed balance for the Haar measure.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Since the staple sum is the expensive part of an update, it pays to use it more than once. The sixth example describes how.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-hits}
#### Several hits per staple

With the staple sum computed once, several Metropolis proposals for the same link can be tested at almost no extra cost, since each needs only one product $U'\Sigma$; in the limit of many hits the link is drawn from its conditional distribution, which is the heat-bath update of @def-lgt-heat-bath. The accept-reject loop of @boudreau2018applied [Sec. 24.4.2] for $U(1)$ repeats the draw until acceptance for the same reason.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The staple also determines the classical field equations of the lattice theory. The seventh example writes them, the lattice Yang-Mills equations.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-eom}
#### The lattice field equations

A configuration is stationary for $S_W$ when, for every link and every $X$ in the Lie algebra, $\frac{d}{d\epsilon}S_W[e^{\epsilon X}U_\mu(x)]|_{\epsilon = 0} = -\frac\beta N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(XU_\mu(x)\Sigma_\mu(x)) = 0$, that is, when the traceless anti-Hermitian part of $U_\mu(x)\Sigma_\mu(x)$ vanishes. For $U(1)$ this is $\sum_P\pm\sin\theta_P = 0$ over the plaquettes through each link, a lattice form of $\partial_\nu F_{\nu\mu} = 0$ (@exr-lgt-st-maxwell), and in the continuum limit the Yang-Mills equations of @def-yang-mills-action.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Links that do not share a plaquette can be updated simultaneously. A two-colouring of the sites tells which, and the figures of this part use it.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-checkerboard}
#### Checkerboard updates

Two links in the same direction $\mu$ share a plaquette only if their sites differ by $\pm a\hat\nu$ with $\nu \neq \mu$, which changes the parity of $\sum_\alpha x_\alpha/a$. So the links in direction $\mu$ at the even sites are conditionally independent given all the others, and can be updated at once; then those at the odd sites, then the next direction (@exr-lgt-st-checkerboard). The Sage scripts of the figures update whole arrays this way.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Staples are also used to smooth configurations before measuring large operators. The procedure, APE smearing, replaces each link by a projected average of itself and its staples.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-ape}
#### APE smearing

APE smearing replaces $U_\mu(x)$ by the projection onto the group of $U_\mu(x) + \zeta\Sigma_\mu(x)^\dagger$ and iterates $n_\zeta$ times; since $U\Sigma \approx k$ near a smooth configuration, $\Sigma^\dagger$ points in the direction of $U$, and the smeared link is a local average of the transports from $x + a\hat\mu$ to $x$. With $\zeta = 0.3$ and $n_\zeta = 8$ [@boudreau2018applied, Exercise 24.14] the smeared links have a transverse size of a few lattice spacings and overlap better with glueballs (@exr-lgt-st-ape).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The staple sum transforms under gauge transformations like a link running backwards. This is what makes the product $U\Sigma$ covariant, as the tenth example shows.

::: {#exm-lgt-st-gauge}
#### Gauge covariance of the staple

Under @eq-lgt-gauge-transformation, each staple in @eq-lgt-staple runs from $x + a\hat\mu$ back to $x$, so $\Sigma_\mu(x) \mapsto g(x + a\hat\mu)^{-1}\Sigma_\mu(x)g(x)$ and $U_\mu(x)\Sigma_\mu(x) \mapsto g(x)^{-1}U_\mu(x)\Sigma_\mu(x)g(x)$: the trace in @eq-lgt-staple-action is gauge invariant, and so is the conditional distribution of the link, up to the corresponding change of variables (@exr-lgt-st-gauge).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The local form of the action follows from collecting the plaquettes that contain the link. The first exercise does this.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-derive}
#### The local action

Show that the plaquettes containing $U_\mu(x)$ are $U_{\mu\nu}(x)$ and $U_{\mu\nu}(x - a\hat\nu)$ for $\nu \neq \mu$, and that their contribution to $S_W$ is $-\frac\beta N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(U_\mu(x)\Sigma_\mu(x))$ plus a constant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U_{\mu\nu}(x) = U_\mu(x)\bigl(U_\nu(x + a\hat\mu)U_\mu(x + a\hat\nu)^{-1}U_\nu(x)^{-1}\bigr)$, the first staple. $U_{\mu\nu}(x - a\hat\nu)$ contains $U_\mu(x)^{-1}$; its real trace equals that of its inverse $U_\nu(x - a\hat\nu)U_\mu(x)U_\nu(x - a\hat\nu + a\hat\mu)^{-1}U_\mu(x - a\hat\nu)^{-1}$, which by cyclicity is $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(U_\mu(x)U_\nu(x + a\hat\mu - a\hat\nu)^{-1}U_\mu(x - a\hat\nu)^{-1}U_\nu(x - a\hat\nu)\bigr)$, the second staple. Summing over $\nu$ and multiplying by $-\beta/N$ gives @eq-lgt-staple-action.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

With Sage, sum six random $SU(2)$ matrices, compute $k = \sqrt{\det\Sigma}$ and $V = \Sigma/k$, check that $V \in SU(2)$ and that $k$ equals the length of the sum of the quaternions, and verify $\frac12\operatorname{Tr}(U\Sigma) = k\,a_0(UV)$.

A proposed change of one link changes the action by an amount that the staple determines. The fourth exercise writes it.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-local}
#### The change of the action

Show that replacing $U_\mu(x)$ by $U'$ changes the Wilson action by $\Delta S = -\frac\beta N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl((U' - U_\mu(x))\Sigma_\mu(x)\bigr)$, and evaluate it for $\mathbb{Z}_2$ when the link is reversed.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only the terms of @eq-lgt-staple-action depend on the link, and they are linear in it. For $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $U' = -\sigma$, so $\Delta S = -\beta(-2\sigma)s = 2\beta\sigma s$: reversing a link aligned with its staple sum costs $2\beta|s|$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The staple sum transforms covariantly, like a link that runs from $x + a\hat\mu$ back to $x$. The fifth exercise proves the law of @exm-lgt-st-gauge from @eq-lgt-gauge-transformation.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-gauge}
#### The staple under gauge transformations

Show that each term of @eq-lgt-staple transforms as $g(x + a\hat\mu)^{-1}(\cdot)g(x)$, and deduce that the conditional distribution of $U_\mu(x)$ given the other links is carried to the conditional distribution for the transformed configuration by $U \mapsto g(x)^{-1}Ug(x + a\hat\mu)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Each staple is the transport along a path from $x + a\hat\mu$ to $x$, so it transforms with $g(x + a\hat\mu)^{-1}$ on the left and $g(x)$ on the right (@exr-lgt-link-path-endpoints). Then $\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(U'\Sigma') = \operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}(U\Sigma)$ for $U' = g(x)^{-1}Ug(x + a\hat\mu)$, and the Haar measure is invariant under this change of variables.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $U(1)$ the stationarity condition of the action is a lattice form of Maxwell's equations without sources. The sixth exercise derives it from @exm-lgt-st-eom.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-maxwell}
#### The lattice Maxwell equations

For $U(1)$, show that $\frac{\partial S_W}{\partial\theta_\mu(x)} = \beta\sum_{\nu \neq \mu}\bigl(\sin\theta_{\mu\nu}(x) - \sin\theta_{\mu\nu}(x - a\hat\nu)\bigr)$, and that setting it to zero gives $\sum_\nu\Delta^-_\nu F_{\mu\nu} = 0$ to leading order in $a$, with the backward difference $\Delta^-_\nu$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\theta_{\mu\nu}(x)$ contains $+\theta_\mu(x)$ and $\theta_{\mu\nu}(x - a\hat\nu)$ contains $-\theta_\mu(x)$, so differentiating $\beta\sum(1 - \cos\theta_P)$ gives the stated sum. With $\theta_{\mu\nu} = a^2eF_{\mu\nu}$, $\sin\theta_{\mu\nu} \approx a^2eF_{\mu\nu}$, and the equation becomes $a^3e\sum_\nu\Delta^-_\nu F_{\mu\nu} = 0$, the Euclidean Maxwell equation $\partial_\nu F_{\nu\mu} = 0$ without sources.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The checkerboard update requires that links of the same direction on sites of equal parity do not interact. The eighth exercise proves it.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-checkerboard}
#### Independence on a checkerboard

Show that the staple sum $\Sigma_\mu(x)$ does not contain any link $U_\mu(y)$ with $y \neq x$ of the same parity as $x$, on a periodic lattice with an even number of sites in each direction. Why is the evenness needed?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The links in @eq-lgt-staple in direction $\mu$ are $U_\mu(x \pm a\hat\nu)$, at sites of the opposite parity; the others are in directions $\nu \neq \mu$. On a periodic lattice with an odd number $L$ of sites in direction $\nu$, the step from $x_\nu = L - 1$ to $0$ does not change the parity in the same way as the others, and two sites of equal parity can be neighbours, so the colouring fails.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The conditional distribution of a $U(1)$ link is a von Mises distribution. The ninth exercise identifies it and its mean.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-von-mises}
#### The conditional distribution of a $U(1)$ link

With $\Sigma = ke^{i\varphi}$, show that $\psi = \theta + \varphi$ has the density $\frac{e^{\beta k\cos\psi}}{2\pi I_0(\beta k)}$ on the circle, and that $\langle\cos\psi\rangle = \frac{I_1(\beta k)}{I_0(\beta k)}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By @exm-lgt-st-u1 the conditional weight of $\theta$ is $e^{\beta k\cos(\theta + \varphi)}\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}$, and the shift $\psi = \theta + \varphi$ preserves the measure; the normalisation $\frac1{2\pi}\int e^{\beta k\cos\psi}d\psi = I_0(\beta k)$ and the mean follow as in @exm-lgt-u1-one-plaquette, with $\beta k$ in place of $\beta$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Smearing makes a configuration smooth by averaging each link with its staples. The tenth exercise applies it to a random configuration with Sage.

::: {#exr-lgt-st-ape}
#### Smearing a random configuration

With Sage, apply eight steps of APE smearing with $\zeta = 0.3$ to a random $SU(2)$ configuration on a periodic $8 \times 8$ lattice, projecting to $SU(2)$ by normalising the quaternion, and follow the average plaquette.

The average plaquette rises from about $0$ to $0.99$: smearing removes the fluctuations at the scale of the lattice spacing and keeps only the long-wavelength content, which is what an operator for a large physical state needs:

{{< sage exr-lgt-st-ape >}}

The staple reduces the update of a link to sampling from a simple distribution on the group. Drawing from it exactly, rather than proposing and testing, is the heat-bath method, and the definition states it with the explicit forms for the three groups.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-lgt-heat-bath}
#### Heat-bath update

A **heat-bath update** of the link $(x, \mu)$ replaces $U_\mu(x)$ by an element drawn from its conditional distribution given all other links,
$$
dp(U) \propto \exp\Bigl(\frac\beta N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}\bigl(U\Sigma_\mu(x)\bigr)\Bigr)dU,
$$ {#eq-lgt-heat-bath}
independently of its previous value; a **sweep** updates every link once. For $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $\sigma = +1$ with probability $\frac{e^{\beta s}}{2\cosh\beta s}$, $s = \Sigma_\mu(x)$. For $U(1)$ with $\Sigma_\mu(x) = ke^{i\varphi}$, $\theta + \varphi$ has the density $\propto e^{\beta k\cos(\theta + \varphi)}$. For $SU(2)$ with $\Sigma_\mu(x) = kV$, $W = UV$ has the density $\propto e^{\beta ka_0(W)}dW$: one draws $a_0 \in [-1, 1]$ with density $\propto\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}\,e^{\beta ka_0}$ and a uniform direction for $\vec a$, and sets $U = WV^{-1}$ [@boudreau2018applied, eqs. 24.44, 24.59 and 24.70-24.71].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For $\mathbb{Z}_2$ the heat bath is a coin with a bias set by the staple. The first example writes the update as programmed by Boudreau and Swanson.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-z2}
#### The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ heat bath

Compute $s$, draw $r$ uniform in $[0, 1]$, and set $\sigma = +1$ if $r < \frac{e^{\beta s}}{e^{\beta s} + e^{-\beta s}}$, otherwise $-1$ [@boudreau2018applied, eq. 24.44]. It is the Glauber update of the Ising model (@exr-tsb-detailed-balance) with the local field replaced by the staple sum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $U(1)$ the conditional density is a von Mises distribution, which can be drawn by rejection. The second example describes the simple method of the source and its cost.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-u1}
#### The $U(1)$ heat bath

Draw $\psi$ uniform on $(-\pi, \pi]$ and accept it with probability $e^{\beta k(\cos\psi - 1)}$, repeating until acceptance; then $\theta = \psi - \varphi$ [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 24.4.2]. The acceptance is $e^{-\beta k}I_0(\beta k) \approx (2\pi\beta k)^{-1/2}$ at large $\beta k$ (@exr-lgt-hb-u1-sampler), and library routines for the von Mises distribution, used in @fig-lgt-two-dim, avoid the loss.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

For $SU(2)$ Creutz reduced the heat bath to a one-dimensional distribution for the component $a_0$. The third example describes his method of drawing it.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-creutz}
#### Creutz's $SU(2)$ heat bath

With $x = \beta k$, the density of $a_0$ is $\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}\,e^{xa_0}$ on $[-1, 1]$. Creutz draws $z = e^{xa_0}$ uniformly in $[e^{-x}, e^x]$, which gives $a_0$ the density $\propto e^{xa_0}$, and accepts with probability $\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}$; a uniform direction completes $W$, and $U = WV^{-1}$ [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 24.5.1]. The acceptance is $\frac{\pi I_1(x)}{2\sinh x}$, which falls like $\sqrt{\pi/2x}$ at large $x$ (@exr-lgt-hb-acceptance).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

At the couplings of interest the Creutz method rejects often. Kennedy and Pendleton found a draw whose acceptance stays high, and the fourth example gives it.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-kp}
#### The Kennedy-Pendleton heat bath

Draw uniform $\eta_1, \dots, \eta_4 \in (0, 1)$, set $\delta = -\frac{\log\eta_1 + \cos^2(2\pi\eta_2)\log\eta_3}{x}$, and accept $a_0 = 1 - \delta$ if $\eta_4^2 \leq 1 - \frac\delta2$ [@boudreau2018applied, Exercise 24.11]. The variable $\delta$ has a $\Gamma(\frac32)$ distribution with density $\propto\sqrt\delta\,e^{-x\delta}$, and the test supplies the factor $\sqrt{1 - \delta/2}$, since $\sqrt{1 - a_0^2} = \sqrt{2\delta}\sqrt{1 - \delta/2}$; the acceptance tends to $1$ as $x$ grows (@exr-lgt-hb-kp).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Heat-bath updates are local, and successive configurations are strongly correlated at weak coupling. Overrelaxation moves a link as far as possible without changing the action.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-overrelax}
#### Overrelaxation

For $SU(2)$ with $\Sigma = kV$, the map $U \mapsto V^{-1}U^{-1}V^{-1}$ preserves $a_0(U\Sigma)$, so it leaves the action unchanged and is always accepted; it reflects the link through the point $V^{-1}$ that minimises the local action [@boudreau2018applied, eq. 24.72 and Exercise 24.10]. Alternating it with heat-bath sweeps reduces autocorrelations at little cost, as the reflection $\phi \mapsto 2\bar\phi - \phi$ did for the scalar field (@exr-fpi-mc-balance).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A Markov chain must be run long enough to forget its starting point. Comparing a cold start with a hot start is the simplest test of thermalisation.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-starts}
#### Cold and hot starts

A cold start sets every link to $1$, the classical vacuum, and a hot start draws every link from the Haar measure, the configuration at $\beta = 0$. Their averages must agree after thermalisation; near a first-order transition they may stay apart for a long time, a hysteresis that signals metastability [@boudreau2018applied, Sec. 24.3.2 and Exercise 24.6]. In @fig-lgt-z2-monte-carlo the two starts agree at every $\beta$, as befits the continuous transition of the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory is the first test case of Boudreau and Swanson. The seventh example compares our simulation with the expansions.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-z2-3d}
#### The three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ plaquette

In @fig-lgt-z2-monte-carlo the average plaquette follows $t + 2t^5$ up to $\beta \approx 0.6$, rises steeply near $\beta_c = 0.7614$, where the duality formula of @exr-lgt-z2-duality-plaquette gives $0.949$, and follows $1 - 8e^{-8\beta} - 88e^{-12\beta}$ above $\beta \approx 0.9$, as in Fig. 24.7 of @boudreau2018applied. The plaquette is not an order parameter; the transition shows in the Wilson loops (@exr-lgt-int-z2-3d) and in the Polyakov loop.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Successive configurations of a Markov chain are correlated, and the correlation grows near a critical point. The eighth example quantifies it for the plaquette.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-autocorrelation}
#### Critical slowing down

The integrated autocorrelation time $\tau_{\text{int}}$ of an observable is estimated from the growth of its blocked error with the block length, as for @def-fpi-metropolis. For the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ plaquette on $8^3$, $\tau_{\text{int}}$ is below one sweep at $\beta = 0.4$ and about $20$ sweeps at $\beta = 0.76$ (@exr-lgt-hb-z2-3d): near a continuous transition the correlation length grows and local updates become slow, critical slowing down, visible in the right panel of @fig-lgt-z2-monte-carlo.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Quarks enter the lattice path integral through the determinant of a matrix that depends on all links. Local heat-bath updates are then impractical, and the simulations use a global algorithm.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-fermions}
#### Dynamical fermions

Integrating out the quark fields leaves the weight $\prod_f\det M_f[U]\,e^{-S_W[U]}$, with $M_f$ the lattice Dirac operator of flavour $f$, which couples all links [@williams2023introduction, eqs. 9.2.66-9.2.68]. The change of the determinant under a single-link update is not local, and production codes use the hybrid Monte Carlo algorithm, which moves all links together along a molecular-dynamics trajectory and corrects with a Metropolis test; the quenched approximation $\det M = 1$ of early work reduces the problem to the pure gauge updates of this section.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The heat bath and the Metropolis update are two ends of one family of local updates. The tenth example states the relation between them.

::: {#exm-lgt-hb-metropolis-limit}
#### Heat bath as many Metropolis hits

Repeated Metropolis hits on one link with a fixed staple form a Markov chain on $G$ with stationary distribution @eq-lgt-heat-bath; as the number of hits grows the final value becomes independent of the initial one and is distributed as the heat bath draws it. For a group as small as $\mathbb{Z}_2$, one heat-bath step is cheaper than two Metropolis hits; for $SU(3)$, where no direct draw exists, a few hits or the $SU(2)$-subgroup heat bath of @exm-lgt-su2-su3 are used.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The heat bath must leave the Boltzmann distribution invariant. The first exercise proves detailed balance for a single-link update, generalising @exr-tsb-detailed-balance.

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-detailed-balance}
#### Detailed balance

Show that a heat-bath update of one link satisfies detailed balance with respect to $e^{-S_W}\prod dU$, and that a sweep therefore leaves this distribution invariant.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For configurations $\mathcal U$ and $\mathcal U'$ that differ only at the link $\ell$, the transition density is $p(\mathcal U \to \mathcal U') = e^{-S_W[\mathcal U']}/\int_GdU\,e^{-S_W[\mathcal U_{\ell \to U}]}$, and the denominator depends only on the other links, which are common to both. Hence $e^{-S_W[\mathcal U]}p(\mathcal U \to \mathcal U') = e^{-S_W[\mathcal U]}e^{-S_W[\mathcal U']}/D = e^{-S_W[\mathcal U']}p(\mathcal U' \to \mathcal U)$. Each single-link update preserves the distribution, and so does their composition, a sweep (which as a whole need not satisfy detailed balance).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ heat-bath probability follows directly from the local form of the action. The second exercise derives it and evaluates it for an aligned link.

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-z2-probability}
#### The $\mathbb{Z}_2$ conditional probability

From @eq-lgt-staple-action, show that the conditional probability of $\sigma_\mu(x) = +1$ is $\frac{e^{\beta s}}{2\cosh\beta s}$, and compute it for $s = 4$ at $\beta = 1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The conditional weights are $e^{\beta\sigma s}$ for $\sigma = \pm1$, so $P(+1) = \frac{e^{\beta s}}{e^{\beta s} + e^{-\beta s}}$. For $s = 4$, $\beta = 1$: $\frac{1}{1 + e^{-8}} = 0.99966$, so an aligned link flips with probability $3.4 \times 10^{-4}$, the $e^{-8\beta}$ of the weak-coupling expansion.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The density of $a_0$ in the $SU(2)$ heat bath comes from the Haar measure on the three-sphere. The third exercise derives it with its normalisation.

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-creutz-density}
#### The density of $a_0$

Starting from $dW = \frac1{\pi^2}\delta(|a|^2 - 1)d^4a$ and the weight $e^{xa_0}$, integrate over the direction of $\vec a$ and show that $a_0$ has the density $\frac{2}{\pi}\frac{\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}\,e^{xa_0}}{2I_1(x)/x}$ on $[-1, 1]$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For fixed $a_0$, $\vec a$ lies on the sphere of radius $\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}$; integrating $\delta(a_0^2 + r^2 - 1)r^2dr\,d\Omega$ gives $2\pi\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}$, so the density is $\frac{2}{\pi}\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}$ (the Weyl measure in $a_0 = \cos\psi$), times $e^{xa_0}$, normalised by $\frac2\pi\int_{-1}^1\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}e^{xa_0}da_0 = \frac{2I_1(x)}{x}$ (@exm-lgt-su2-one-plaquette).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

Overrelaxation preserves the action exactly. The fifth exercise proves it and finds the order of the map [@boudreau2018applied, Exercise 24.10].

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-overrelax}
#### The overrelaxation map

For $SU(2)$ and $\Sigma = kV$, show that $U' = V^{-1}U^{-1}V^{-1}$ satisfies $a_0(U'\Sigma) = a_0(U\Sigma)$ and $U'' = U$, and that the map preserves the Haar measure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$U'\Sigma = kV^{-1}U^{-1}V^{-1}V = kV^{-1}U^{-1} = k(UV)^{-1}$, and $a_0$ of an $SU(2)$ element equals $a_0$ of its inverse, so the local action is unchanged. Applying the map twice, $V^{-1}(V^{-1}U^{-1}V^{-1})^{-1}V^{-1} = V^{-1}VUVV^{-1} = U$. The map is the composition of inversion and left and right translations, each of which preserves the Haar measure, so it is a measure-preserving involution that keeps the action fixed; it satisfies detailed balance with acceptance one.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A hot start draws every link from the Haar measure. The seventh exercise shows that this is the heat bath at $\beta = 0$ and computes the starting plaquette.

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-hot-start}
#### The hot start

Show that at $\beta = 0$ the heat bath draws each link from the Haar measure, independently of everything else, and that the average plaquette of a hot start is $0$ in expectation for $\mathbb{Z}_2$, $U(1)$ and $SU(2)$. What is the spread of the average over $n_P$ plaquettes for $SU(2)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At $\beta = 0$ the weight @eq-lgt-heat-bath is $1$, so the draw is the Haar measure. A plaquette of independent Haar links is itself Haar distributed (a product with independent Haar factors), so $\langle\frac1N\operatorname{Re}\operatorname{Tr}U_P\rangle = 0$. For $SU(2)$, $\langle a_0^2\rangle = \frac14$ (@exr-lgt-wa-haar-su2), so the average over $n_P$ independent plaquettes has standard deviation $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{n_P}}$, about $0.06$ for the $64$ plaquettes of an $8 \times 8$ lattice, consistent with the starting value $-0.02$ of @exr-lgt-st-ape.
:::

#### Autocorrelation near the transition

With Sage, run the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ heat bath on a periodic $8^3$ lattice for $2000$ sweeps at $\beta = 0.4$ and $\beta = 0.76$, estimate the error of the average plaquette from blocks of $1, 5, 25, 100$ sweeps, and estimate $\tau_{\text{int}} \approx \frac12(\text{error}_{100}/\text{error}_1)^2$.

Creutz's method rejects more and more often at weak coupling, where the staple is large. The ninth exercise computes its acceptance exactly with Sage.

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-acceptance}
#### The acceptance of Creutz's method

Show that the acceptance of Creutz's draw is $\frac{\int_{-1}^1\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}e^{xa_0}da_0}{\int_{-1}^1e^{xa_0}da_0} = \frac{\pi I_1(x)}{2\sinh x}$, evaluate it with Sage for $x$ from $0.5$ to $50$, and compare with $\sqrt{\pi/2x}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The proposal has density $\propto e^{xa_0}$ and is accepted with probability $\sqrt{1 - a_0^2}$, whose average is the ratio; the integrals are $\frac{\pi I_1(x)}{x}$ and $\frac{2\sinh x}{x}$. At large $x$, $I_1(x) \approx e^x/\sqrt{2\pi x}$ and the acceptance tends to $\sqrt{\pi/2x}$, $0.18$ at $x = 50$:

{{< sage exr-lgt-hb-acceptance >}}
:::

The cost of a lattice simulation is dominated by the staples. The tenth exercise estimates the work of one sweep.

::: {#exr-lgt-hb-cost}
#### The cost of a sweep

For $SU(2)$ on a $16^4$ lattice, count the links, the products of two quaternions needed for one staple sum, and the real multiplications of one sweep. How long does a sweep take at $10^9$ multiplications per second?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are $4 \cdot 16^4 = 262\,144$ links. A staple sum has $6$ staples of $2$ quaternion products each, $12$ products, and the heat bath adds $2$ more; a quaternion product has $16$ real multiplications, so a link costs about $14 \cdot 16 = 224$ multiplications and a sweep about $5.9 \times 10^7$, some $0.06$ s, so that a thousand sweeps, enough for the plaquette and small loops, take about a minute.
:::

### Exercises {#sec-lattice-gauge-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Three exercises combine the sections of this part, one for each of the groups. The first follows two-dimensional compact $U(1)$ from the definition to its continuum limit, the second locates the transition of the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory by its Wilson loops, and the third assembles the evidence that four-dimensional $SU(2)$ confines.

The first integrative exercise uses the exact solution of the second section, the area law of the third and the heat bath of the fifth. Its Monte Carlo is a check of the whole chain of definitions on a case where the answer is known.

::: {#exr-lgt-int-2d-u1}
#### Two-dimensional compact $U(1)$ from start to finish

For compact $U(1)$ on a two-dimensional lattice: (a) show that the Wilson loops obey $W(C) = (I_1(\beta)/I_0(\beta))^A$; (b) with $\beta = 1/(e^2a^2)$, find the continuum string tension and compare with Gauss's law; (c) simulate the theory with Sage on a $12 \times 12$ torus at $\beta = 2$ with the von Mises heat bath, and compare $W(1, 1)$, $W(2, 2)$, $W(2, 3)$ with $u^A$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) By @prp-lgt-two-dim and the lattice Stokes theorem (@exr-lgt-2d-abelian-loop). (b) $\hat\sigma = \log(I_0/I_1) = \frac{1}{2\beta} + O(\beta^{-2})$, so $\sigma = \hat\sigma/a^2 \to \frac{e^2}{2}$, the field energy per unit length of @exr-lgt-al-gauss-2d. (c) The measured loops agree with $u^A$, $u = I_1(2)/I_0(2) = 0.698$, within one or two standard deviations, the finite-size effects of the torus being of order $u^{144}$:

{{< sage exr-lgt-int-2d-u1 >}}

The second integrative exercise uses the strong-coupling expansion, the duality of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ section and the Monte Carlo of the last section. It shows the area and the perimeter laws on the two sides of a transition.

::: {#exr-lgt-int-z2-3d}
#### The two phases of the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory

For the three-dimensional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ theory: (a) give the strong-coupling string tension and the weak-coupling perimeter coefficient; (b) locate the transition by duality; (c) measure $W(1, 1)$, $W(1, 2)$, $W(2, 2)$ with Sage on an $8^3$ lattice at $\beta = 0.25$ and $\beta = 1$, compute the Creutz ratio $\chi(2, 2)$, and decide in each case whether $-\log W$ scales with the area or with the perimeter.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\hat\sigma = -\log\tanh\beta - 2\tanh^4\beta + \dots$ (@exm-lgt-sc-bump), and $\hat\mu \approx 2e^{-8\beta}$ per unit length (@exr-lgt-al-z2-perimeter). (b) $\beta_c = \operatorname{arctanh}e^{-2K_c} = 0.7614$ (@exr-lgt-z2-dual-3d). (c) At $\beta = 0.25$, $-\log W/A \approx 1.40$ for the three loops and $\chi(2, 2) = 1.42$, close to $-\log\tanh0.25 = 1.41$: an area law. At $\beta = 1$, $-\log W/P \approx 0.0009$ for the three loops and $\chi(2, 2) \approx 0$: a perimeter law. The two phases are separated by $\beta_c$:

{{< sage exr-lgt-int-z2-3d >}}

The third integrative exercise combines the continuum limit of the first section, the $SU(2)$ theory of the second, the strong-coupling expansion and the heat bath. It reconstructs the argument by which lattice simulations established confinement in a non-abelian gauge theory.

::: {#exr-lgt-int-su2}
#### Confinement in four-dimensional $SU(2)$

For four-dimensional $SU(2)$: (a) simulate the theory with Sage on a $4^4$ lattice with the Kennedy-Pendleton heat bath at $\beta = 0.5$ and $\beta = 4$, and compare the average plaquette with $\frac\beta4$ and $1 - \frac{3}{4\beta}$; (b) give the strong-coupling string tension with its first correction; (c) explain why the scaling form $\hat\sigma \propto e^{-6\pi^2\beta/11}$ follows from asymptotic freedom, and find the lattice spacing at $\beta = 2.5$ from $\sigma = 0.18$ GeV$^2$ with the normalisation of @fig-lgt-strong-coupling; (d) explain why (b) and (c) together are evidence that the continuum theory confines, while the same reasoning fails for compact $U(1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) The plaquette is $0.1235$ at $\beta = 0.5$, against $\frac\beta4 = 0.125$, and $0.80$ at $\beta = 4$, against $1 - \frac{3}{16} = 0.8125$, the difference being the next order in $1/\beta$. (b) $\hat\sigma = -\log u - 4u^4 + \dots$ with $u = I_2(\beta)/I_1(\beta) \approx \frac\beta4$ (@exm-lgt-sc-bump). (c) At fixed physical $\sigma$, $\hat\sigma = \sigma a^2$, and asymptotic freedom gives $a \propto e^{-3\pi^2\beta/11}$ (@exm-lgt-cl-asymptotic-freedom), so $\hat\sigma \propto e^{-6\pi^2\beta/11}$; at $\beta = 2.5$, $\hat\sigma = 0.068$ and $a = 0.12$ fm. (d) The strong-coupling area law holds for every compact group, but only if no phase transition intervenes does it reach the continuum limit at $\beta \to \infty$; for $SU(2)$ the two forms join smoothly near $\beta \approx 2.1$ (@exm-lgt-sc-crossover, @exm-lgt-su2-scaling), while compact $U(1)$ has a transition at $\beta_c \approx 1.01$ beyond which the area law is lost (@exm-lgt-sc-u1-paradox):

{{< sage exr-lgt-int-su2 >}}
:::

## The Standard Model {#sec-standard-model}

The first three parts built the general machinery: gauge fields for any compact group (@sec-yang-mills), the anomaly condition that chiral fermions must satisfy (@def-gth-anomaly-coefficient), spontaneous symmetry breaking (@sec-ssb) and the Higgs mechanism (@sec-higgs), and, on the lattice, confinement. The Standard Model of particle physics is one particular choice inside this machinery: the gauge group $SU(3) \times SU(2) \times U(1)$, three copies of a set of fifteen chiral fermions with fixed hypercharges, and one scalar doublet whose vacuum breaks $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to electromagnetism. Nothing in this part is new as mathematics. What is new is that each choice is forced, or nearly so, by consistency and by experiment, and that the resulting formulas can be compared with measured masses, widths and couplings.

For more on this topic, see @nath2017supersymmetry [Ch. 5], @pal2015introductory [Chs. 12 and 16-19] and @paganini2023fundamentals [Chs. 8-12].

This part has four sections and a set of integrative exercises. The first fixes the gauge group, its three couplings and the representations in which fields transform, and treats the unbroken colour factor, quantum chromodynamics, whose coupling decreases at high energies. The second lists one generation of quarks and leptons with their hypercharges, and proves that the cancellation of gauge anomalies fixes the hypercharges up to normalisation. The third breaks $SU(2) \times U(1)$ with the Higgs doublet of @sec-higgs, defines the weak mixing angle and derives the masses of the $W$ and $Z$ bosons and their relation to the Fermi constant. The fourth gives the quarks their masses through Yukawa couplings and shows that the mismatch between the mass basis and the weak basis is a unitary matrix, the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa matrix, with a single phase that violates CP. The sources are @nath2017supersymmetry [Ch. 5 and Sec. 6.10], @pal2015introductory [Chs. 12 and 16-19] and @paganini2023fundamentals [Chs. 8, 9 and 11].

The conventions are those of the chapter. Generators are anti-Hermitian, $T_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A$ for $SU(3)$ with the Gell-Mann matrices of @def-gell-mann and $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$ for $SU(2)$; their Hermitian partners are $t = iT$, and the weak isospin $T_3$ of a component is its eigenvalue of $t_3 = \tfrac12\sigma_3$. The Higgs doublet has the vacuum $\phi_0 = (0, v)$ of @exm-higgs-su2-masses, so that our $v \approx 174$ GeV is $1/\sqrt2$ times the $v \approx 246$ GeV of the three sources, whose formulas are converted accordingly; @nath2017supersymmetry also uses the signature $(-, +, +, +)$, which changes the signs of his kinetic terms. Fermions are chiral fields $\psi_L$, $\psi_R$ (@def-dq-weyl-equation), and a right-handed field in a representation counts for anomalies as a left-handed field in the conjugate representation (@def-gth-anomaly-coefficient).

### The gauge group and its representations {#sec-smd-group}

![Left: the weights $(t_3, t_8)$, the eigenvalues of $\tfrac12\lambda_3$ and $\tfrac12\lambda_8$, of the colour triplet $\mathbf3$ (the quark colours $r$, $g$, $b$), of the antitriplet $\bar{\mathbf3}$ and of the octet $\mathbf8$ of gluons, whose weights are the differences of triplet weights, two of them at the origin. Right: the one-loop running of the strong coupling from $\alpha_s(m_Z) = 0.118$ with $b_0 = 11 - \tfrac23n_f$, the number of flavours changing at $m_b = 4.18$ GeV and $m_t = 172.7$ GeV, compared with fifty times the electromagnetic $\alpha(Q)$ run from $1/137.036$ with the charged fermions lighter than $Q$: $\alpha_s$ falls while $\alpha$ rises. At one loop $\alpha_s(m_\tau) = 0.28$, below the measured $0.33$, because the higher-loop terms are omitted. Generated by `figures/sm_qcd.sage`.](figures/sm_qcd.svg){#fig-sm-qcd width=95%}

The gauge group is the first choice the Standard Model makes. It is a product of three factors, each with its own coupling, and a field is specified by an irreducible representation of each factor; the general construction of @def-covariant-derivative-nonabelian is applied once for each factor. The definition fixes the group, the gauge fields and the covariant derivative, and the examples treat the colour factor, which stays unbroken and makes up quantum chromodynamics.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-smd-gauge-group}
#### Standard Model gauge group

The **Standard Model gauge group** is the direct product $G_{\rm SM} = SU(3)_C \times SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ of colour, weak isospin and hypercharge, with gauge fields $G^A_\mu$ ($A = 1, \dots, 8$), $W^a_\mu$ ($a = 1, 2, 3$) and $B_\mu$ and three couplings $g_s$, $g$ and $g'$. A field transforms in an irreducible representation $(\mathbf r, \mathbf s)_y$: $\mathbf r$ of $SU(3)$, $\mathbf s$ of $SU(2)$, labelled by their dimensions, and a **hypercharge** $y \in \mathbb{Q}$, on which the $U(1)$ generator acts as $Y = -iy$. Its covariant derivative (@def-covariant-derivative-nonabelian) is
$$
D_\mu = \partial_\mu + g_sG^A_\mu\rho_{\mathbf r}(T_A) + gW^a_\mu\rho_{\mathbf s}(T_a) - ig'yB_\mu ,
$$ {#eq-smd-covariant-derivative}
with $T_A = -\tfrac{i}{2}\lambda_A$ (@def-gell-mann) and $T_a = -\tfrac{i}{2}\sigma_a$, and the gauge fields have the Yang-Mills Lagrangian $-\tfrac14G^A_{\mu\nu}G^{A\,\mu\nu} - \tfrac14W^a_{\mu\nu}W^{a\,\mu\nu} - \tfrac14B_{\mu\nu}B^{\mu\nu}$ in the canonical normalisation of @def-nonabelian-field-strength, each field strength containing its own coupling [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 5.1-5.3, 5.6-5.7 and 5.58; @pal2015introductory, Secs. 12.1 and 16.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A gauge group fixes the number of gauge bosons, and the count is the first thing to compare with experiment. The first example counts them before and after the electroweak breaking of @sec-smd-electroweak.

::: {#exm-smd-group-count}
#### Twelve gauge bosons

$\dim G_{\rm SM} = 8 + 3 + 1 = 12$, as noted in @exm-nonabelian-su3. After the breaking of $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ by the Higgs doublet, nine of them stay massless, the eight gluons and the photon, and three become massive, the $W^+$, the $W^-$ and the $Z$; the unbroken group is $SU(3)_C \times U(1)_{\rm em}$ [@pal2015introductory, eq. 16.17].
:::

The covariant derivative of a doublet shows how the weak isospin and the hypercharge act together. The second example writes it for the lepton doublet, the multiplet of the electron and its neutrino.

::: {#exm-smd-group-lepton-doublet}
#### The covariant derivative of a lepton doublet

The lepton doublet $L_L = (\nu_L, e_L)$ is a colour singlet with $\mathbf s = \mathbf2$ and $y = -\tfrac12$. @eq-smd-covariant-derivative gives
$$
D_\mu L_L = \partial_\mu L_L - \frac{i}{2}\begin{pmatrix} gW^3_\mu - g'B_\mu & g(W^1_\mu - iW^2_\mu) \\ g(W^1_\mu + iW^2_\mu) & -gW^3_\mu - g'B_\mu \end{pmatrix}L_L ,
$$
the matrix of @pal2015introductory [eqs. 16.34-16.35] in our sign convention: the off-diagonal entries turn a neutrino into an electron and back, and the diagonal ones do not change the particle.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

A field that is a singlet of both non-abelian factors feels only the hypercharge. The third example is the right-handed electron, which is such a field.

::: {#exm-smd-group-singlet}
#### A singlet feels only the hypercharge

The right-handed electron $e_R$ is $(\mathbf1, \mathbf1)_{-1}$, so $D_\mu e_R = (\partial_\mu + ig'B_\mu)e_R$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 5.7]: neither the gluons nor the $W^a$ act on it. The two chiralities of the electron therefore have different gauge interactions, which is possible because they are different representations of the Lorentz group (@def-dq-weyl-equation) [@pal2015introductory, Sec. 16.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

A quark carries both a colour index and, when left-handed, an isospin index. The fourth example shows how the two non-abelian factors act on such a field without interfering.

::: {#exm-smd-group-quark}
#### A left-handed quark doublet

The quark doublet $Q_L$ is $(\mathbf3, \mathbf2)_{1/6}$: a field $Q^{i\alpha}_L$ with a colour index $i = 1, 2, 3$ and an isospin index $\alpha = 1, 2$, six complex components for each spinor index. The covariant derivative acts as $\rho(T_A) = T_A \otimes \mathbb{1}_2$ and $\rho(T_a) = \mathbb{1}_3 \otimes T_a$, and the two sets commute, $[T_A \otimes \mathbb{1}, \mathbb{1} \otimes T_a] = 0$, as the generators of a direct product must; the two-generation form of the same derivative is @nath2017supersymmetry [eq. 5.48].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The colour group could in principle have been another group with a three-dimensional representation. The fifth example gives the argument that singles out $SU(3)$.

::: {#exm-smd-group-why-su3}
#### Why colour is $SU(3)$

Quarks come in three colours, so the colour group needs an irreducible three-dimensional representation. Among unitary groups only $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ have one; the triplet of $SU(2)$ is its adjoint, which is real, so quarks and antiquarks would have the same colour properties. The triplet of $SU(3)$ is complex, $\mathbf3 \not\cong \bar{\mathbf3}$, and its weights $(\pm\tfrac12, \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3})$ and $(0, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$ are the negatives of those of $\bar{\mathbf3}$ (@fig-sm-qcd) [@pal2015introductory, Sec. 12.1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The gluons transform in the adjoint representation, so they carry colour themselves. The sixth example reads this off the weights and the generators.

::: {#exm-smd-group-gluons}
#### Gluons carry colour

The adjoint $\mathbf8$ is $\mathbf3 \otimes \bar{\mathbf3}$ minus a singlet, so its weights are the differences of triplet weights: six non-zero roots and two zero weights (@fig-sm-qcd, @def-root). The combinations $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lambda_1 \pm i\lambda_2)$, $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lambda_4 \pm i\lambda_5)$ and $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\lambda_6 \pm i\lambda_7)$ each have a single non-zero entry and move one colour into another, while $\lambda_3$ and $\lambda_8$ are diagonal and leave colours unchanged [@pal2015introductory, eqs. 12.3-12.4]. A charged gluon is the analogue of a charged photon, which is why gluons interact with each other (@exr-gth-ym-cubic-quartic).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Observed hadrons carry no colour. The seventh example finds the colour-singlet combinations of quarks and antiquarks, which are the states that confinement allows.

::: {#exm-smd-group-hadrons}
#### Colour singlets

$\mathbf3 \otimes \bar{\mathbf3} = \mathbf8 \oplus \mathbf1$, with singlet $\bar q_iq^i$: a meson. $\mathbf3 \otimes \mathbf3 \otimes \mathbf3 = \mathbf{10} \oplus \mathbf8 \oplus \mathbf8 \oplus \mathbf1$, with the totally antisymmetric singlet $\epsilon_{ijk}q^iq^jq^k$: a baryon [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 1.15; @paganini2023fundamentals, eq. 8.20]. $\mathbf3 \otimes \mathbf3 = \mathbf6 \oplus \bar{\mathbf3}$ has no singlet, so two quarks cannot form a colourless state. On the lattice, only colour singlets have finite energy at strong coupling (@sec-lgt-confinement).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The strong interactions are the colour part of the Standard Model taken alone. The eighth example writes their Lagrangian, which is the special case of the gauge-group definition with only $SU(3)$ kept.

::: {#exm-smd-group-qcd}
#### The Lagrangian of quantum chromodynamics

Ignoring $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$, the strong interactions are
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\rm QCD} = -\tfrac14G^A_{\mu\nu}G^{A\,\mu\nu} + \sum_q\bar q(i\gamma^\mu D_\mu - m_q)q, \qquad D_\mu = \partial_\mu + g_sG^A_\mu T_A ,
$$
summed over the six quark flavours, each a colour triplet [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 5.58; @paganini2023fundamentals, Sec. 8.2]. The colour symmetry is exact and unbroken; the masses depend on the flavour but not on the colour, so that the approximate flavour symmetries of the quark model (@exm-lrep-branch-hypercharge) are global and broken by mass differences. The theory also admits the $\theta$ term of @exr-gth-theta-total-derivative.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The coupling $g_s$ is not constant but depends on the energy at which it is measured. The ninth example gives the one-loop coefficient that controls this dependence, quoted for pure Yang-Mills theory in @exm-rn-asymptotic-freedom, now with quarks.

::: {#exm-smd-group-asymptotic-freedom}
#### Asymptotic freedom with quarks

At one loop $Q\frac{d\alpha_s}{dQ} = -\frac{b_0}{2\pi}\alpha_s^2$, $\alpha_s = g_s^2/4\pi$, with $b_0 = \frac{11}{3}C_A - \frac43T_Fn_f$, where $C_A = N$ for $SU(N)$, $T_F = \tfrac12$ for the fundamental representation, and $n_f$ counts Dirac fermions in it. For $SU(3)$, $b_0 = 11 - \frac23n_f$, which is positive for $n_f \leq 16$: the coupling decreases at high energies and grows at low ones [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 5.59-5.61; @paganini2023fundamentals, Sec. 8.4]. The six known quarks are far below the limit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Integrating the one-loop equation gives the coupling at any scale from its value at one scale. The tenth example evaluates it between the $Z$ mass and the $\tau$ mass, and compares it with the electromagnetic coupling.

::: {#exm-smd-group-running}
#### The running couplings

The one-loop equation integrates to $\frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q)} = \frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q_0)} + \frac{b_0}{2\pi}\log\frac{Q}{Q_0}$ [@paganini2023fundamentals, eq. 8.103]. From $\alpha_s(m_Z) = 0.118$ with $n_f = 5$ it gives $\alpha_s(m_b) = 0.212$ at $m_b = 4.18$ GeV, and with $n_f = 4$ below, $\alpha_s(m_\tau) = 0.279$, while the measured value is about $0.33$; the difference is the two-loop and higher terms. The electromagnetic coupling has the opposite sign of $b_0$ and grows, from $1/137.036$ at low energy to $1/127.95$ at $m_Z$ (@fig-sm-qcd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The definition is mostly bookkeeping, and the exercises make the bookkeeping explicit. The first one rewrites @eq-smd-covariant-derivative with Hermitian generators, the form used by the sources.

::: {#exr-smd-group-hermitian}
#### The Hermitian form of the covariant derivative

Show that @eq-smd-covariant-derivative is $D_\mu = \partial_\mu - i(g_sG^A_\mu t_A + gW^a_\mu t_a + g'yB_\mu)$ with Hermitian $t = iT$, and that the kinetic term $\bar\psi i\gamma^\mu D_\mu\psi$ of a Dirac field contains the interaction $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu(g_sG^A_\mu t_A + gW^a_\mu t_a + g'yB_\mu)\psi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$T = -it$, so $g_sG^AT_A = -ig_sG^At_A$, and likewise for $W$; the hypercharge term is already $-ig'yB$. Then $i\gamma^\mu D_\mu = i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu + \gamma^\mu(g_sG^At_A + gW^at_a + g'yB)$, because $i \cdot (-i) = 1$. This is the derivative of @nath2017supersymmetry [eq. 5.6], $\partial_\mu - igT^aA^a_\mu - iYg'B_\mu$, while @pal2015introductory [eq. 16.4] uses the opposite sign of all couplings.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The hypercharge of a field and the coupling $g'$ enter only through their product. The second exercise draws the consequence for the normalisation of $y$.

::: {#exr-smd-group-rescaling}
#### Rescaling the hypercharge

Show that replacing every hypercharge by $cy$ and $g'$ by $g'/c$ leaves all covariant derivatives unchanged. What fixes $c$ in the Standard Model?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Only $g'y$ appears in @eq-smd-covariant-derivative, and $(g'/c)(cy) = g'y$. The normalisation is therefore a convention; it is fixed by requiring that the unbroken electric charge be $Q = T_3 + y$ with no coefficient in front of $y$ [@pal2015introductory, Sec. 16.3.1, after eq. 16.18], which gives the hypercharges of @def-smd-generation. In grand unified theories a different normalisation, $y_1 = \sqrt{3/5}\,y$, is natural (@exr-smd-gen-traces).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

All fields share a single abelian gauge field, whatever their hypercharge. The third exercise checks that the gauge transformation of $B_\mu$ does not depend on which field one looks at.

::: {#exr-smd-group-abelian-transformation}
#### The gauge transformation of the hypercharge field

For $g(x) = e^{\alpha(x)Y}$ with $Y = -iy$, a field of hypercharge $y$ transforms as $\psi \mapsto e^{iy\alpha}\psi$ (@def-covariant-derivative-nonabelian). Find the transformation of $B_\mu$ that keeps $D_\mu\psi$ covariant, and show that it is the same for all $y$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $-ig'yB_\mu$ in $D_\mu$, $D_\mu(e^{iy\alpha}\psi) = e^{iy\alpha}\bigl(\partial_\mu + iy\partial_\mu\alpha - ig'yB_\mu\bigr)\psi$, which equals $e^{iy\alpha}D_\mu\psi$ after $B_\mu \mapsto B_\mu + \frac{1}{g'}\partial_\mu\alpha$. The factor $y$ cancels, so one field $B_\mu$ couples consistently to all hypercharges, with strengths $g'y$; this is the abelian gauge transformation of @def-gauge-field-u1 with the coupling made explicit.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The weights in @fig-sm-qcd are the joint eigenvalues of two commuting generators. The fourth exercise computes them for the three colour representations of the Standard Model.

::: {#exr-smd-group-weights}
#### Weights of the colour representations

With Sage, compute the joint eigenvalues of $t_3 = \tfrac12\lambda_3$ and $t_8 = \tfrac12\lambda_8$ on the triplet, of $-t_3^T$ and $-t_8^T$ on the antitriplet, and of the adjoint generators $(t_A)_{BC} = -if_{ABC}$ on the octet, and compare with the figure.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The triplet has $(\pm\tfrac12, \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt3})$ and $(0, -\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3})$, the antitriplet their negatives, and the octet the six differences $(\pm1, 0)$, $(\pm\tfrac12, \pm\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2})$ together with $(0, 0)$ twice, as drawn in @fig-sm-qcd:

{{< sage exr-smd-group-weights >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The one-loop coefficient $b_0$ contains two group-theory numbers, $C_A$ and $T_F$. The fifth exercise computes them, together with the Casimir of the triplet.

::: {#exr-smd-group-casimir}
#### Casimirs of the colour representations

With Sage, compute $\sum_At_At_A$ and $\operatorname{Tr}(t_At_B)$ for the triplet and the adjoint of $SU(3)$, check $C_2(R)\dim R = T(R)\dim G$, and recover $b_0 = 11 - \tfrac23n_f$ from the formula of @exm-smd-group-asymptotic-freedom.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The triplet has $C_F = \tfrac43$ and $T_F = \tfrac12$; the adjoint has $C_A = T(\mathbf8) = 3$. Indeed $\tfrac43 \cdot 3 = \tfrac12 \cdot 8$ and $3 \cdot 8 = 3 \cdot 8$. Then $\tfrac{11}{3} \cdot 3 - \tfrac43 \cdot \tfrac12n_f = 11 - \tfrac23n_f$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, eqs. 5.60-5.61]:

{{< sage exr-smd-group-casimir >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The colour singlets of @exm-smd-group-hadrons are built from the invariant tensors $\delta^i_j$ and $\epsilon_{ijk}$. The sixth exercise checks their invariance numerically.

::: {#exr-smd-group-singlets}
#### Invariant tensors of $SU(3)$

With Sage, draw a random $U \in SU(3)$ and check that $\epsilon_{ijk}U_{il}U_{jm}U_{kn} = \epsilon_{lmn}$ and that $\bar q \cdot p$ is invariant for two triplets. Show also that $\epsilon_{ijk}q^jp^k$ transforms as an antitriplet, and explain why this rules out a colourless diquark.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\epsilon_{ijk}U_{il}U_{jm}U_{kn} = \det U\,\epsilon_{lmn} = \epsilon_{lmn}$, and $(Uq)^\dagger Up = q^\dagger p$ since $U$ is unitary. For two quarks the only invariant tensor available, $\epsilon_{ijk}$, leaves one index free, and $\epsilon_{ijk}(Uq)^j(Up)^k = (\bar U)_{il}\epsilon_{lmn}q^mp^n$ by the same determinant identity, a $\bar{\mathbf3}$; a singlet needs a third quark [@nath2017supersymmetry, eq. 1.15]:

{{< sage exr-smd-group-singlets >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The sign of $b_0$ depends on the number of quark flavours, and too many would destroy asymptotic freedom. The seventh exercise finds the limit for $SU(N)$.

::: {#exr-smd-group-flavours}
#### How many flavours can QCD have?

Find the largest number of Dirac fermions in the fundamental representation of $SU(N)$ for which $b_0 > 0$, for $N = 2$ and $N = 3$. How does a left-handed Weyl fermion in the fundamental count?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$b_0 = \tfrac{11}{3}N - \tfrac23n_f > 0$ requires $n_f < \tfrac{11}{2}N$: $n_f \leq 10$ for $SU(2)$ and $n_f \leq 16$ for $SU(3)$ [@nath2017supersymmetry, after eq. 5.61]. A Weyl fermion has half the degrees of freedom of a Dirac fermion and contributes half as much, so $n_f$ counts Weyl fermions with weight $\tfrac12$; in one generation $Q_L$, $u^c$ and $d^c$ supply four Weyl triplets or antitriplets, two Dirac flavours.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The running coupling at one scale fixes it at all scales, and the comparison with measurements tests the one-loop formula. The eighth exercise runs $\alpha_s$ from the $Z$ mass to the $\tau$ mass and extracts the scale at which it would diverge.

::: {#exr-smd-group-running}
#### Running $\alpha_s$ down to the $\tau$ mass

With Sage, run $\alpha_s$ at one loop from $\alpha_s(m_Z) = 0.118$ to $m_b = 4.18$ GeV with $n_f = 5$ and on to $m_\tau = 1.777$ GeV with $n_f = 4$. Then use the measured $\alpha_s(m_\tau) = 0.33$ to find $\Lambda = Q_0e^{-2\pi/(b_0\alpha_s(Q_0))}$ for $n_f = 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The one-loop values are $\alpha_s(m_b) = 0.212$ and $\alpha_s(m_\tau) = 0.279$, below the measured $0.33$, as in @fig-sm-qcd. From $\alpha_s(m_\tau) = 0.33$, $\Lambda^{(4)} = 0.18$ GeV, the "about 200 MeV" of @paganini2023fundamentals [eq. 8.104 and the text after it], a length of about $1$ fm, the size of a hadron; the same formula with $\alpha_s(m_Z) = 0.118$ and $n_f = 5$ gives $\Lambda^{(5)} = 0.088$ GeV:

{{< sage exr-smd-group-running >}}
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The scale $\Lambda$ of the previous exercise was defined from one reference point, but it does not depend on which one is used. The ninth exercise proves this and rewrites the coupling in terms of $\Lambda$ alone.

::: {#exr-smd-group-lambda}
#### Dimensional transmutation

Show from the one-loop solution of @exm-smd-group-running that $\Lambda = Q_0\exp\bigl(-\frac{2\pi}{b_0\alpha_s(Q_0)}\bigr)$ is the same for every $Q_0$, and that $\alpha_s(Q) = \frac{2\pi}{b_0\log(Q/\Lambda)}$. Why does this formula fail for $Q \lesssim \Lambda$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q)} - \frac{b_0}{2\pi}\log Q = \frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q_0)} - \frac{b_0}{2\pi}\log Q_0$ is independent of the scale; call it $-\frac{b_0}{2\pi}\log\Lambda$. Then $\frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q)} = \frac{b_0}{2\pi}\log\frac{Q}{\Lambda}$, and solving for $\Lambda$ at $Q = Q_0$ gives the formula [@paganini2023fundamentals, eq. 8.104]. The dimensionless coupling has been traded for a mass scale. The formula diverges at $Q = \Lambda$, where perturbation theory has long ceased to be valid; below it the lattice of @sec-lattice-gauge is needed.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The abelian factor behaves in the opposite way to the colour factor. The tenth exercise runs the electromagnetic coupling up to the $Z$ mass and finds the limits of the one-loop estimate.

::: {#exr-smd-group-alpha-em}
#### Running the fine-structure constant

At one loop, each charged fermion lighter than $Q$ contributes $-\frac{2}{3\pi}N_cQ_f^2\log\frac{Q}{m_f}$ to $1/\alpha(Q)$, starting from $1/\alpha = 137.036$ at low energy [@paganini2023fundamentals, eq. 8.103 with $C_A = 0$ and the footnote to it]. With Sage, evaluate $1/\alpha(m_Z)$ with the three charged leptons and the five quarks lighter than $m_Z$, and compare with $127.95$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The leptons shift $1/\alpha$ by $4.84$ and the quarks by $5.62$, giving $1/\alpha(m_Z) = 126.6$, within $1.2\%$ of $127.95$. The discrepancy comes from the light quarks: their contribution is non-perturbative, and their masses are not the right cut-offs, so the hadronic part is in practice taken from data:

{{< sage exr-smd-group-alpha-em >}}
:::
